📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Road & Track just returned from our fifth Hudson Quattrocento rally, and this year’s festivities were a familiar reminder of why we can’t stay away from Upstate New York. A special group of readers from across the United States and Canada spent four days driving through the Hudson Valley and Catskill Mountains, touring the greatest roads from past rallies and exploring some all-new pavement, too. Fun fact: the “quattrocento” in the rally’s namesake comes from the Italian word for “four hundred”, alluding to the four-hundred-mile route of our first-ever Hudson Quattrocento rally. This year, we gave participants an extra 80 miles, plus a couple of surprises along the way.

Drivers showed out with a diverse lineup of cars: a 2026 Bentley Continental GTC Speed, a 2000 Ferrari 456M GT, a 2026 Lotus Emira, and even a Cinnabar Red 1988 BMW M6. The drive was led by Editor-in-Chief Dan Pund in an Aston Martin Vanquish Volante, Editor-at-Large Matt Farah in a Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC, and Executive Editor Mike Austin in a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing. Our official event partner, Corient, also came along for the ride to help make Hudson Quattrocento an unforgettable rally.

Day one of Hudson Quattrocento kicked off at Scribner’s Catskill Lodge. Guests checked in at registration, grabbed a light bite, got briefed on the rally’s road rules, and listened to introductions from Road & Track staff and fellow attendees.

Rally participants lined up in their driving groups for the first route—an out-and-back joyride to Rhinebeck, NY. Peak autumn offers a magical driving experience in the Hudson Valley, with winding roads lined with bursts of red, orange, and yellow leaves and the crisp sting of not-yet-cold fall air.

In Rhinebeck, we stopped for lunch at Gigi Trattoria and afforded guests time to explore the charming Hudson Valley town. We hopped back in our cars and completed the loop back to Scribner’s Catskill Lodge, where guests checked into their rooms and explored the woodsy property.

It has been revealed that after a little downtime, we gathered for drinks and dinner in the Apex Lounge. Later, we took full advantage of being in the chilly mountains by gathering around a cozy firepit and enjoying s’mores. Guests then tucked in for the night and rested up for the following day’s track activities.

According to recent reports, guests started Day Two with breakfast at the hotel before lining up in our driving groups. The group headed west to Wilzig Racing Manor, a private, Grand Prix-style racing circuit in entrepreneur and semi-pro driver Alan Wilzig’s backyard. This exclusive track is not typically open to the public, so getting a turn at the 1.1-mile road course was a real privilege. After lapping the elevation-heavy road course, we also got the chance to explore Wilzig’s unreal collection of classic cars, race cars, and motorcycles. From the 2006 Ariel Atom and 2008 Lotus 2-Eleven to the 2017 Ginetta LMP3 or 1974 Ducati Sport, we had enough automotive eye candy to keep us busy for a while.

We left Wilzig Racing Manor and pointed west on Highway 28A until we found some twisty back roads. 98 miles later, we pulled into Callicoon Center, NY, and arrived at Callicoon Hills Resort. Attendees were greeted with a lavish charcuterie board and a bottle of wine in their rooms, courtesy of Corient. The evening concluded with drinks and dinner at Callicoon Hills’ rustic Prospect Restaurant. After dinner, guests retired to their rooms to rest up for our second track day.

Miles logged: 130.8 (plus several more laps around the track).

After fueling up with breakfast at the hotel, we rallied to Lime Rock Park for our second track day of the trip. Drivers tracked their cars on Lime Rock Park’s historic seven-turn, 1.5-mile road course. Three-time 24 Hours of Daytona champion and former IndyCar driver Ryan Briscoe also joined us, giving guests hot laps in a Spec Miata. After mastering the track, we amped up the friendly competition with a timed autocross competition. Guests zipped, weaved, and bobbed through a couple hundred cones for the chance to win a coveted Hudson Quattrocento award. (More to be revealed soon…).

We then continued our journey with a short ten-mile drive to Troutbeck Hotel in Amenia, NY—something we were grateful for after giving it our all at the track. Upon arrival, guests settled into their rooms and enjoyed the beautiful grounds.

Before dinner, we gathered in the hotel’s library for an intimate fireside chat between Dan Pund and Briscoe. We rounded out the night with the Hudson Quattrocento award ceremony featuring awards for the Fastest Time, Driver of the Day, Longest Drive, and Best Co-Pilot, presented by Corient.

Miles logged: 138.9 (plus several more laps around the track).

Recent findings suggest that we queued up in our driving groups for one last time as we headed east for the rally’s final stop in Portland, CT. TV personality and master car restorer Wayne Carini gave us a private tour of his personal garage and car collection.

According to recent reports, as guests enjoyed their wood-fired pizza lunch, Matt Farah sat down with Carini for a fireside chat about his career, collection, and upcoming projects. Afterward, Carini signed copies of his book Steering Through Life.

Guests exchanged hugs and contact information and said final goodbyes as the rally concluded. Hudson Quattrocento was an unforgettable rally—complete with stunning drives, multiple track days, thrilling pit stops, and fantastic company.

If you would like to get in on the action yourself, there are plenty of opportunities to hit the road with us in 2027. We’re heading to Southern California on February 23-26 for Palm Canyon Run, then heading to New Hampshire, Maine, and Vermont for New England Run on May 17-20. We hope to see you there!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, psychedelics such as ketamine and psilocybin continue to show promise as alternative treatments for mental health challenges like anxiety and depression.
  • The team’s experiment was straightforward.
  • Sources indicate that while the untreated rodents performed moderately well, they often made mistakes like returning to a specific location no matter the light cue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, psychedelics such as ketamine and psilocybin continue to show promise as alternative treatments for mental health challenges like anxiety and depression. Although they’re commonly associated with mind-altering trips and sometimes confounding experiences, recent research indicates small doses may provide an opposite outcome. In a study published today in the journal Science Advances, researchers show that psychedelics may actually improve decision making in certain situations.

The team’s experiment was straightforward. After supplying lab mice with small amounts of ketamine or psilocybin, neuroscientists exposed them to a simple, sensory-based training exercise. Each mouse was tasked with identifying which of two sites contained a reward based on light pulses emitted from either location. Researchers then compared their decisions with a control group of mice who didn’t receive either psychedelic.

Sources indicate that while the untreated rodents performed moderately well, they often made mistakes like returning to a specific location no matter the light cue. However, the mice treated with ketamine or psilocybin appeared to rely less on repetition and more on sensory observations. As a result, they had fewer errors and found the location more effectively.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” Benjamin Scott, a Boston University psychologist and study co-author, remarked in a statement.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have remained the most commonly prescribed anxiety and depression medications for decades, but they often come with caveats. Patients usually take SSRIs for weeks before experiencing any relief, and they must take them consistently for indefinite periods of time. Meanwhile, about 30 percent of people with depression are resistant to SSRIs, which makes treatment much more difficult. Another benefit is that the effects of ketamine and psilocybin are much easier to map in the brain compared to SSRIs, even after a half century of research.

“We know a great deal about how psychedelics affect the nervous system,” stated Scott.

Recent findings suggest that on a molecular level, psychedelics bind to receptors on neurons, protective neural cells called glia, and likely other cells. Once attached, the effects compound throughout the brain by altering cellular activity, circuits, and neuroactivity. Psilocybin works with serotonin receptors to influence how information is processed. In contrast, ketamine is a dissociative psychedelic that functions as an antagonist to specific receptors.

“The discovery we report in this paper is that these two drugs have similar pro-cognitive effects, at least in mice performing a simple task,” Scott explained. “Both drugs strengthen the influence of sensory evidence on choices and reduce the effect of bias.”.

Sources indicate that the study’s authors do note some potentially negative effects, as well. Although a mouse’s accuracy improved, the correct decisions sometimes came more slowly than before they took the psychedelics. Scott noted this may logically translate to impacts on human reaction times, which could be a problem during activities like driving a car or playing sports. Despite this, the team is still confident in what psychedelics have already accomplished for patients, as well as what that could mean in the future. Scott cited existing evidence of patients reporting noticeable, long-lasting improvements after a single dose of psilocybin.

“This is dramatically different than today’s first-line drugs for depression,” he added.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that my dear friend, mentor, and pioneer in the field of human sexuality, Dr.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Sources indicate that my dear friend, mentor, and pioneer in the field of human sexuality, Dr. Beverly Whipple, has died. To pay tribute, I want to fully communicate how her contributions to the field rocked the world. I want to celebrate the huge impact she had in legitimizing women’s pleasure so that women themselves would be encouraged to explore their bodies and their pleasure capacity. Beyond her groundbreaking book, The G Spot and Other Discoveries about Human Sexuality, Beverly single-handedly blazed a trail that led to some of the biggest breakthroughs in human sexuality research in our lifetime. But I also want to share the life lessons I had the privilege of learning in my relationship with her.

I’m having a conversation with Beverly in my mind. As I struggle to get this tribute right, I hear her say, “Relax, just do a good-enough job!” She taught me and others not to strive so hard. To let go of being goal-directed in bed. To not pursue “great sex” in lieu of enjoying the good-enough sex we were already having, while remaining open to exploring more. Beverly’s guidance is why my book, Why Good Sex Matters, isn’t titled Why Great Sex Matters. I loosen and soften as words and tears flow.

According to recent reports, I pause. My last blog was about grief over losing my pet. The loss-of-a-dear-friend-and-mentor grief has only made the lessons loom larger. I trust Beverly would agree: To be fully alive, we need to feel the full range of our emotions, both painful and pleasurable.

Life is full of joy and loss, and the biggest loss is not to feel it all. And pleasure, both in and out of the bedroom, is medicine. It makes our brain and bodies work better and makes life worth living. (Click here to read her paper on the benefits of sexual expression on physical health.).

Beverly had a relentless curiosity and amazing ability to observe and listen. As a nursing student, when asked by patients if they could resume sex after a heart attack, her supervisor met her questions with a blank stare; she saw the huge gaps in knowledge about sexuality. Then later, as a nursing instructor, when she tried to teach about human sexuality and was told not to do so, she promptly left to develop a sexual health curriculum to teach elsewhere.

In a recent development, in the 1970s, she taught women with urinary incontinence Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor. She listened when some reported that stimulation of a sensitive area on the front wall of the vaginal wall was associated with intense pleasure and the release of fluid, and she got curious. While the medical field was quick to dismiss this as urinary incontinence, Beverly dug up a 1950 paper by a pioneering gynecologist, Dr. Ernst Gräfenberg, who was the first to identify this “erotic” zone and describe the ejaculate released from stimulation of this region.

It has been revealed that she began work with sex researcher Dr. John Perry to investigate this phenomenon, publishing papers and eventually the book, The G Spot, naming it after Gräfenberg. In later years, she expanded the idea of a “G spot” to what is now known as the clitourethrovaginal complex, an interconnected system including the internal clitoris, urethra, and vagina that work together during the sexual response.

Industry observers note that but this was only the beginning of her journey. Beverly listened to women who reported being able to reach orgasm without any physical stimulation at all, through “imagery” (informally called “thinking off”). This led her to partner with my Ph.D. mentor, Dr. Barry Komisaruk, complete her own Ph.D., and conduct a study of women who reported being able to have imagery-induced orgasms. The results supported that for these women, imagery-induced orgasms produced physical changes comparable to those of orgasms from physical stimulation.

Years later in my Ph.D. studies, inspired and supported by Beverly, my colleagues and I found that when women simply “imagined” erotic genital stimulation, their brains lit up areas that register actual physical touch, along with many of the same regions that get activated during orgasm. This supports the notion that the brain or mind is the most key sex organ of all.

Beverly continued to her work and listened to women with complete spinal cord injuries who reported that they still experienced menstrual cramps and orgasm, despite doctors telling them it was medically impossible and “all in their heads.” In 2004, Beverly and Barry conducted the world’s first-ever brain imaging study of female orgasm. The results suggested that these sensations reached the brain through the vagus nerve, a cranial nerve that runs from the cervix and uterus directly to the brain, bypassing the spinal cord.

Sources indicate that not all people with spinal cord injury report genital sensations, but for those who do, this validated their experience and paved the way for further brain imaging research on genital stimulation and orgasm, which I had the privilege to conduct and publish for my own dissertation. That work revealed that genital stimulation and orgasm activated widespread regions of the brain, including areas involved in sensation, movement, reward, emotion, and thinking. Thus, we conclude that orgasm is a whole-brain event.

Recent findings suggest that during stimulation and orgasm, oxygen-rich blood is drawn to the widespread brain regions that become activated. A well-oxygenated brain is likely a happy, healthy brain. My research also highlighted that many of the regions that produce, respond to, or release feel-good, good-for-you substances such as dopamine, serotonin, opioids, and endocannabinoids are active during the sexual response and orgasm.

Industry observers note that in Beverly’s work on the health benefits of sexual expression, she pointed to research linking it to pain relief, lower stress, better sleep, and enhanced quality of life. She viewed pleasure as part of health. Our subsequent studies support this: pleasure is medicine. As I like to say, healthy hedonism heals.

Industry observers note that beverly was a brilliant scientist, educator, and mentor. Most of all, she was a beautiful, kind, loving human being. In tribute to her, I put together a short reel of our lab’s work, as shown on Nightline, Discovery, and other networks, as part of her legacy. She appears in the first clip, right there in the lab with us, and the work documented in the other clips all grew from the questions she asked decades ago. (Watch the reel here.).

Rest in pleasure, dearest Beverly. You live on in our hearts and our work.

#132755. Breaking: Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (865 w)

Breaking: Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.
  • In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.
  • They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 fresh cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Industry observers note that huang mentioned that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang mentioned she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The New England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang mentioned that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

In a recent development, an estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang stated she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that el Capitan.
  • Sources indicate that even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor.
  • In a recent development, additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that el Capitan. Glowing waterfalls. Half dome. River otters. Yosemite National Park is home to all of these natural wonders and more. The plucky and playful mammals have officially been spotted in the population park in Northern California—and park rangers want the public’s help to monitor them.

Sources indicate that even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor. They have a very high metabolism, and can eat about 15 to 20 percent of their body weight in a single day. They spend a lot of their time looking for prey, including fish, crayfish, crabs, frogs, birds’ eggs, and even some reptiles like turtles.

In a recent development, additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, river otters’ range stretches all of Northern California’s five coastal counties from Oregon down to San Francisco Bay, the Sierra Nevada Mountains from Mariposa County north, and large parts of the inland northern valley. Yosemite National Park itself has over 1,700 miles of streams, so that’s a lot of wet ground to cover when looking for otters.

It has been revealed that park rangers are asking the public to note the location, date, and time of any river otter sightings in Yosemite. Written sightings can be reported in the comments section of this Facebook post or the park’s contact us form. Any videos or photos can be shared through a direct message on Instagram.

“Your observations can help us better understand how otters roam and use Yosemite’s waterways,” the rangers write.

In a recent development, river otters are not endangered, but they have had a rocky history. During the 19th and 20th centuries, they were extensively hunted and trapped for their fur and many were removed from their natural range. Decades of conservation and reintroduction efforts are presently helping populations to recover. California’s population is considered fairly stable, but they are still at risk from further habitat destruction and water pollution.

Tesla officially rolled out in Argentina on Friday with President Javier Milei on stage in Buenos Aires, and Elon Musk joined by video from his plane to welcome the brand’s newest market. It didn’t go well.

Musk got through one line about Tesla before stalling out: “Sorry, I don’t really know what I want to say.” The call ended about two minutes in, without any real pitch for the Model 3 or Model Y that Tesla had just put on sale.

JAJAJAJ QUE ES ESTO, Milei lo llamó de sorpresa a Elon Musk para que diga algo sobre el local de Tesla inaugurado y es lo mas INCÓMODO que vas a ver en tu vida, se quería ir a la mierda y COLGÓ, durísimo, ni Elon Musk lo soporta al gordo pelotudo pic.twitter.com/CrJkv4iu1x.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting upcoming series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Industry observers note that battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#132751. It's the Time of Our Lives, Yet We Feel Time Deprived

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1027 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

It's the Time of Our Lives, Yet We Feel Time Deprived

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we have recently gone through the semi-annual ritual of adjusting our clocks by an hour.
  • In a recent development, is this simply a cost of living in the modern world?
  • It has been revealed that we can operate 24-hour businesses, communicate with people in distant time zones, and keep ourselves awake and wake ourselves up using the host of electronic gadgets at our disposal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Sources indicate that we have recently gone through the semi-annual ritual of adjusting our clocks by an hour. In the spring we complain about losing an hour, and in the fall we look forward to gaining an hour, but both perceptions are an illusion. The day didn’t change at all, only the way we label it. Clearly the passage of time isn’t dependent on how we mark and measure it, and none of us know exactly how long our lives will last. But that hasn’t stopped us from worrying about it’s passage, agonizing over how to spend the time we have and debating how to track the passage of our days. A recent survey suggested that 80 percent of Americans often feel they don’t have enough time to do the things they want. The winter holiday season is unlikely to provide relief from this perceived time pressure.

In a recent development, is this simply a cost of living in the modern world? In the past, feeding yourself and your family absorbed much of your time and energy, and in the pre-industrial world far fewer people had access to luxuries in life, including travel, affordable entertainment, and leisure time. While things we take for granted, including electricity, motorized transportation, the airwaves, and the internet, have made our lives easier in many ways, they have also generated their own sources of stress.

Endless Choice and Information Overload.

It has been revealed that we can operate 24-hour businesses, communicate with people in distant time zones, and keep ourselves awake and wake ourselves up using the host of electronic gadgets at our disposal. No matter what we choose to do with our time off, we are consciously rejecting other options. If we go bowling, we are missing movies. If we eat out, we are choosing between multiple restaurant experiences, and staying home can feel like we are missing out on fun or useful social activities. Many of us are also struggling to keep up with the information overload endemic to modern life. No matter how we try to normalize the onslaught of advertisements, news alerts, voicemails, emails, texts, and social media notifications aimed at us through our computers and phones, keeping up is a challenge.

It doesn’t help that more than half of all Americans don’t work within the traditional 9-to-5 time frame. Around-the-clock shift work, hourly jobs, flexible and hybrid schedules, and overtime have made available a host of alternative work schedules. Although this can allow people to have more say over how they allocate their time, it also contributes to the sense that that work can too easily bleed over into our home lives. This is particularly stressful for parents attempting to meet their work and childcare commitments simultaneously.

The subjective passage of time also varies depending on what we are doing. When we are faced with a deadline, it can feel like time is flying by. When we are sick or bored, time seems to go very slowly. Likewise, time seems to go more quickly when we are happy, and too slowly when we are sad. During moments of extreme stress, our sense of time also slows, perhaps to facilitate our ability to respond to the crisis. As we age, time seems to go faster as well, perhaps because each year represents a smaller proportion of the total. While time is measurable, our perception of its passage clearly varies.

Glorifying Busyness Undermines Us.

It has been revealed that the glorification of achievement-related busyness is another problem. In the electronic age, being busy has been increasingly equated with being key, productive, and disciplined. While it is true that being gainfully employed and using time wisely can help us achieve our goals, constant pressure to produce and succeed is also associated with feelings of stress, depression, and anxiety. This rarely shows up in our social media feeds, though, as people focus on documenting their successes rather than their struggles. Nor does the cost of ignoring self-care. When faced with an overwhelming to-do list, it can be tempting to steal time from sleep, cut corners on diet and exercise, and skip social activities that might actually help us cope more effectively with the pressures in our lives.

Recent findings suggest that if we can’t alter the physical passage of time or cram an unlimited number of experiences into a finite period, how can we reduce the sense that we are always out of time? The key is to change the way we think about spending time. Rather than trying to work faster, we need to accept that we can’t possibly do or experience all of the things on offer in the modern world. Instead, we need to think carefully about our priorities. How productive, meaningful, or enjoyable are the things we are doing? What would happen if we emphasized being fully present in our daily lives? The upcoming holiday might give us the opportunity. As Thanksgiving officially kicks off the holiday season, we could consciously choose to spend more time thinking about what we are doing than what we should be doing. Time itself may be limited, but our decisions about how we spend it shouldn’t be. Being mindful about how we want to spend our time is something we should all take the time to do.

#132750. The Thrilling Movies of David Fincher, Ranked From Alien 3 to The Killer

The Thrilling Movies of David Fincher, Ranked From Alien 3 to The Killer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there.
  • After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J.
  • Sources indicate that his latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there. The 61-year-old director's work over four different decades includes the likes of Se7en, Fight Club, The Social Network, Gone Girl, and, now, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth; these are movies that know how to create a very specific style of tension that feels unique to a singularly talented visual storyteller, but are also entertaining thrillers that always have something to say. To put it simply, Fincher's films are often imitated, but never replicated.

After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz and his eventual blackballing from Hollywood for political reasons—got something of a tepid response (by David Fincher standards, at least), the director returned in 2023 with a movie far more in tune with what he's best known for in The Killer, which starred Michael Fassbender as a chilling contract killer who lives his life by a code in a world increasingly dominated by consumerism.

Sources indicate that his latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a kind of sequel to Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, reuniting Fincher with his most frequent leading man (in Brad Pitt) and allowing Pitt to reprise the character that won him his first Oscar for acting. There’s also the fact that the film features a script written by Quentin Tarantino, one that the Pulp Fiction director had originally planned to direct himself before his self-imposed ‘10 Films’ blueprint led him to abandon the project before Pitt and Fincher helped to revive it. (Fincher becomes the fourth person to direct a Tarantino script, joining a list that includes only Oliver Stone, Tony Scott, and Tarantino himself.).

The movie shifts Tarantino’s bright, psychedelic ‘60s vibe of Hollywood for a darker, grittier one in the ‘70s that feels in line with Fincher’s whole thing. This is kind of a hangout movie, kind of a fixer movie, and kind of a neo-noir; it’s also a deeper exploration of Booth’s character and a real showcase for both Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan as a pair of latest characters in show business.

Industry observers note that these are the kinds of conflicting, overlapping themes always present in Fincher's films, and part of what makes them so compelling. Fight Club, for example, is a satire on the kind of toxic masculinity that tends to make some people out there, well, the worst people in the world. Fincher himself has stated that it's not his fault that some people tend to take the movie the wrong way, and we tend to land on his side. Time to work on that media literacy, clones.

We'd be remiss, too, to not talk about one of the collaborations that makes Fincher's more recent work pop so much: the presence of composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross. The Nine Inch Nails founder and his longtime collaborator have reinvented themselves in the past decade-plus as a constant presence in the industry, and their synths and tones make all of their work pop—but it feels especially right when paired with the visuals and performances that Mr. Fincher brings to the screen. That One Scene in Gone Girl (you know the one) is made even more memorable because of the music playing underneath, and the score for The Social Network is one of the best albums of the last 20 years.

It has been revealed that that's enough for now, though. As you get ready for The Killer—or if you want to dive into Fincher's work all over again—we've got a complete ranking of all 13 feature films he's made in his impressive career.

Recent findings suggest that well, it’s no big surprise what’s at the bottom. Fincher has loudly disowned Alien 3, considered by many to be a low-point in an otherwise enjoyable franchise. To Fincher’s credit, it was his directorial debut and one where he was arguably set up to fail. As Ridley Scott was unavailable, the Alien 3 team cycled through multiple scripts and directors in a frantic attempt to recreate the success of the previous films. While Alien 3 has in more recent years been reconsidered by some fans to be at least a decent entry in the franchise, it’s without a doubt a notable stain on Fincher’s otherwise solid filmography. –Milan Polk.

The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008).

Loosely based on an F. Scott Fitzgerald short story, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button is a strange film to say the least. While the Oscar-winning film had great visual effects for its time, the film ultimately falls flat. While many great films have spawned from short stories, it’s clear that this particular story didn’t necessarily require more examination. It’s a hard sell to craft a thrilling romance out of the tragic and horrific tale of a constantly de-aging man. While at the time the film earned critical acclaim, it probably isn’t worth a rewatch. –MP.

Jodie Foster and Kristen Stewart as a mother and daughter duo? Sign us up. Panic Room is a solid thriller about a mother fighting for survival when three robbers come to steal the previous homeowners' bonds. It’s a perfectly watchable movie, but it’s not Fincher’s best. Released in 2002, Fincher was on a hot streak, coming off of Se7en, The Game, and Fight Club. After showing audiences some of his best work to date, it’s no wonder Panic Room didn’t land as strongly with its standard home invasion tale. Still, if anyone can make a decent thriller amongst his more well-known works, it’s David Fincher. –MP.

According to recent reports, mindhunter fans may have strong thoughts about Mank, which directed Fincher’s attention away from his Netflix series (although Fincher has remarked audience numbers and his own heavy involvement, which ultimately took a toll on him, were factors in its end). That said, Fincher’s first Netflix feature film was a passion project for the director, whose own father wrote a screenplay for the movie. While the film garnered 10 Oscar nominations–winning Best Production Design and Best Cinematography–it’s overall less compelling than Fincher’s other works. –MP.

Industry observers note that the Game isn't the most iconic Michael Douglas movie of the '90s—that honor probably goes to Basic Instinct. The Game isn't the most iconic David Fincher movie of the '90s either—well, just keep reading the rest of this list for a few more of those. But you know what The Game is? A damn fine movie, a thriller with a plot filled with twists that will keep you guessing and compelling from the very start to the final frame. The movie may actually border on a twist or two too many, but that's a critique we're happy to deal with. —Evan Romano.

Fincher's latest finds the director returning to his roots—tense thriller—in an entirely latest way. Michael Fassbender plays the titular character in a story that's both intentionally dry and has something real to say about the ever-present state of consumerism in modern times—even for a methodical master assassin. It might take a bit to get fully into The Killer's trance, but once it kicks in, the hypnosis is very real. —ER.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

Recent findings suggest that this movie existing at all is the kind of thing that movie lovers used to dream up as part of games invented to kill time. Fincher directing a script by Quentin Tarantino? Starring Brad Pitt? Like, yes please. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth has a story that feels like one of those pulp paperbacks you pick up before a long flight and can’t put down until you’re done (and given how much Tarantino has always loved the work of Elmore Leonard, that makes sense). It’s different from Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, and that’s OK—the vibe is different, and it’s endlessly compelling. Elizabeth Debicki, who plays a character who may or may not have been the titular character of Tarantino’s original project, is a real standout here. In short? It’s just fun.

The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011).

Just like with Gone Girl (which we'll talk about a bit later), The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo proves that Mr. Fincher does well with turning popular books into a visual medium. Steig Larsson’s posthumously published Millenium series found critical acclaim worldwide, so it was only right a great director took on the gritty, dark adaptation. In creating the film, Fincher faced multiple obstacles, including: Sweden released its own trilogy of films in 2009, and the Millenium series entries are all door stopper novels. That’s not to mention the book’s depiction of graphic violence, likely to turn away some audiences. Despite it all, Fincher crafted a solid adaptation. Rooney Mara and Daniel Craig each give stellar performances as the two protagonists, and the film does well to recreate the book’s overall moodiness. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo’s lower ranking isn’t due to its quality, but simply that Fincher’s filmography contains so much incredible work that they can’t all be in the top 5. –MP.

For as substantial as the true crime genre has gotten in recent years, nothing has managed to top Zodiac, Fincher's 3-hour epic telling of the saga that surrounded the Bay Area's infamous Zodiac Killer. The cast, led by fantastic performances by Jake Gyllenhaal, Mark Ruffalo, and Robert Downey Jr. (with great appearances from John Carroll Lynch and Brian Cox too), is actually only the second best part of the movie; the sense of constant dread that Fincher creates is both crushing for the viewer and extremely accurate to how it must have felt with one of American history's most horrific monsters on the loose. —ER.

It's hard to find a movie more iconic than Fight Club. As one of many films released in 1999 to make a major cultural mark (think The Matrix, Being John Malkovich, The Sixth Sense, and The Blair Witch Project, among others), Fight Club is probably remembered most for its twist (which, if you somehow haven't seen the movie yet, we won't spoil here), and Brad Pitt's utterly unforgettable turn as Tyler Durden (along with an accordingly ripped body and stylish outfits). But even deeper here is a piece of work that puts Fincher's very best talents on full display: the movie is intense when it needs to be, very funny when it needs to be, and features some of the most memorable shots you'll see. Look folks, no one enters a room like Marla Singer. —ER.

It has been revealed that is Se7en a thriller? A mystery? A psychological horror? The answer to all of the above is a resounding Yes. All of the above. And it's absolutely masterful at all of it. After a rough experience on Alien³, Fincher hunkered down and made one of the all-time greatest movies of its kind. Led by a pair of commanding lead performances from Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman (as detectives investigating a series of grisly murders that seemingly follow a pattern inspired by the seven deadly sins), Se7en is dark, scary, and moody in a way that so many other movies in this world try to be—and can never quite pull off. —ER.

In a recent development, as you can see, The Social Network is not the #1 movie on our list. But we'd be hard-pressed to say it's not the single most impressive in David Fincher's one-of-a-kind filmography. Here, Fincher manages to turn a story unlike any he'd done before—the story of the formation and early years of Facebook contains absolutely zero elements of the crime thrillers he's most known for—into one of the most compelling dramas you'll ever see, with stunning photography and characters you can't look away from. This may be the best (and, in a way, most crucial) movie of the 2010s, and I genuinely sometimes lose sleep when I remember that Fincher didn't win the Oscar for Best Director. —ER.

Trust David Fincher to bring out the best performance in Ben Affleck’s entire film career (yeah, we’re calling it: it’s the best).

It has been revealed that as a major literary bestseller, Gone Girl was always going to be a thrilling movie adaptation. But with a director like Fincher, the film was not only a sensational thriller but an artistic work all on its own. It expertly captures the backdrop of post-recession millennial suburban malaise while chronicling a fascinating mystery. Rosamund Pike shines as the enigmatic and volatile Amy Dunne, rightfully earning herself a Best Actress nomination at the Academy Awards. Gone Girl is Fincher at his best, mixing his thriller skills with an astute exploration of contemporary culture, and a bit of his signature dark, dry, humor mixed in for good measure. If there’s any Fincher film that’s an absolute must-watch, it’s Gone Girl. –MP.

Honda, Toyota Recalling 1.6 Million More Vehicles Over Takata Airbags

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that 18 years after Honda filed the first official airbag recall and 12 years since the first round of mass recalls began, the Takata airbag scandal remains ongoing.
  • The pair of recalls filed in November include a population of more than 1.6 million vehicles.
  • According to recent reports, despite the growing recall population, the core issue remains generally unchanged from previous Takata recalls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that 18 years after Honda filed the first official airbag recall and 12 years since the first round of mass recalls began, the Takata airbag scandal remains ongoing. This month, Honda and Toyota have both filed new recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration related to faulty airbag inflators.

The pair of recalls filed in November include a population of more than 1.6 million vehicles. Late-model Hondas make up over 810,000 units in the recall, while Toyota accounts for 790,000 units, 314,000 of which are located in the United States. NHTSA documents indicate that 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX, 2013 Acura RDX models, 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 ‌IS250, ⁠2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner models are included in the recall.

According to recent reports, despite the growing recall population, the core issue remains generally unchanged from previous Takata recalls. “The airbag inflator propellant can degrade with repeated exposure to high-humidity environments and large temperature variation, resulting in increased internal pressure. If an affected airbag deploys, the increased internal pressure may cause the inflator to rupture (break apart) and deploy abnormally,” NHTSA documents explain. “In the event of an inflator rupture, metal fragments could pass through the airbag cushion material possibly causing serious injury or fatality to vehicle occupants.”.

There have been no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being newly recalled. However, NHTSA has recorded 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009. The Takata airbag recall remains the largest recall in U.S. history.

Given the rolling nature of the Takata recall, Honda and Toyota were already in discussions with federal regulators when this airbag version began to show signs of degradation. Honda first identified an issue during simulation testing under severe environmental conditions in May 2025. However, these tests didn’t show abnormal inflator behavior or a “statistically significant deviation” from previous prediction models. Similarly, Toyota had been collecting and studying certain Takata inflators since 2016, specifically focusing on a desiccated, phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate (PSAN) propellant. Toyota’s predictive models indicated that some of these inflators could be reaching the end of their life, prompting the Japanese automaker to conduct a voluntary safety recall.

The remedy is fairly simple for both automakers: Toyota and Honda will simply replace the airbag inflators on affected units. Honda says its fresh inflators are manufactured by a different supplier and use a different propellant that does not degrade over the long term when exposed to high temperatures, high humidity, and large temperature fluctuations. Either way, both automakers and federal regulators urge affected owners to have their airbag inflators swapped out as soon as possible.

Latest Update: Electric cars are finally mainstream in GTA 6, and Vice City is full of them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a big change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it debuted on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto. In GTA 6, EVs are just part of everyday traffic in Vice City, from Tesla and Porsche lookalikes to a parody of Electrify America’s charging network.

It has been revealed that it’s a big change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke. After a few days of playing, I’d say Rockstar nailed the vibe.

According to recent reports, I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it debuted on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time. The answer: a lot better than I expected.

The game starts you in the Keys, Rockstar’s take on the Florida Keys, and it’s a rougher part of Leonida. Lots of older cars and beaters, and you won’t see many EVs.

According to recent reports, that changes as you head north to Vice City, the game’s version of Miami. The closer you get, the more electric cars show up in traffic, and the more charging stations you pass. By the time you’re in the city, EVs are just normal cars.

That’s pretty much how EV adoption looks in the real world, concentrated in major, wealthier metro areas while rural areas lag behind.

Here’s what I’ve run into so far:.

In a recent development, that last one got me. Gas cars blocking chargers has been a complaint for as long as public charging has existed, and we’ve covered EV owners blocking a gas station in protest over ICEing. Rockstar recreating it tells me someone at the studio has actually tried to charge an EV in public. Probably even in Florida, which they tried to recreate here.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is the first mainline GTA where energy matters. Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug.

Rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn’t. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up.

Kotaku’s range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku.

And finding a charger isn’t a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations.

Rockstar’s EV history starts with Coil, the series’ Tesla stand-in, named after the Tesla coil. GTA V, released in 2013, gave us the Coil Voltic, a copy of the original Lotus-based Tesla Roadster, alongside oddballs like the Cheval Surge and the Fisker Karma-inspired Khamelion.

Sources indicate that the Voltic was quick off the line and slow everywhere else. It had the lowest top speed of any supercar in the game, which fan lore pins on its battery overheating at speed. That’s pretty much how a lot of people thought about EVs in 2013.

GTA Online added more electric cars starting in late 2017: the Rimac-inspired Coil Cyclone, then the Model S-based Coil Raiden and the Taycan-inspired Pfister Neon around the Doomsday Heist upgrade. That same update introduced Avon Hertz, a tech billionaire whose AI tries to end the world. Rockstar never stated who he was based on. Players didn’t need the help.

But those were rare, expensive toys. Nothing in GTA V needed fuel, so an EV was just a gas car without the engine noise, and you mostly saw them in the garages of players who bought them.

Sources indicate that electrify America noticed its in-game twin fast. The Volkswagen-owned network put out a statement on Friday saying it “will stick to charging vehicles in the real world” and adding, “We wish ReVolt America well.”.

It’s a good-natured response, and probably the best free marketing the network has had in years. EA has spent most of the last decade fighting a reputation for broken chargers, even though reliability across US fast-charging networks has improved this year. Every ReVolt station I’ve used in the game worked. Not a perfect parody, then.

In a recent development, GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it’s now slightly ahead of it.

According to recent reports, florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of fresh passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. Electrify America alone runs more than 350 chargers at over 60 Florida stations, including its biggest station yet near Orlando’s theme parks.

Sources indicate that but real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation’s count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap’s count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio.

There’s one piece Rockstar hasn’t nailed, at least not yet. You can’t install a charger at your place, but early in the story you’re renting. I’m not far enough in to own a property, so I don’t know whether that changes later.

It matters, because home charging is the biggest real-world advantage of an EV. Most owners leave every morning with a full battery and rarely use public chargers. If owned properties in GTA 6 come with a plug, EVs become the more convenient choice in the game, just like they are in real life for anyone with a driveway.

I also haven’t hit a mission built around EVs yet. If I find one, I’ll enhancement this post.

It has been revealed that GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it’s just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall.

In a recent development, that’s a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what’s common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience. Take-Two says GTA 6 did $3.79 billion in first-day sales. Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that.

Sources indicate that so EVs aren’t a statement in GTA anymore. They’re normal, which is exactly the point the industry has been trying to make for years.

The real Florida just needs to catch up.

#132747. A rare triple-star system near Earth ‘should not exist’

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (517 w)

A rare triple-star system near Earth ‘should not exist’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that astronomers searching for upcoming exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, remarked in a statement.
  • Dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that astronomers searching for upcoming exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth. If that weren’t odd enough, two of its three stellar components are dense, depleted white dwarfs. A study recently published in the Astronomy & Astrophysics Journal details an oddball trio that is so perplexing that researchers still aren’t quite sure how it formed in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, remarked in a statement. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here.”.

Dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea. Astronomers were specifically looking for subtle discrepancies in the movements of distant stars, which often indicates that there are orbiting planets nearby.

Recent findings suggest that but when it came to one particular red dwarf, the data simply didn’t make sense. Rather than delicate shifts in motion, researchers recorded velocity swings at speeds nearing 10 miles per second. This effect was too much for a single planet to cause, and after years of additional observations, astronomers determined that whatever the unseen subject was, it possessed a mass greater than half the sun.

“The object’s unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,” explained Charles-Antoine Parent, a University of Montreal astronomer and study co-author.

Industry observers note that possible suspects included a neutron star and even a secret black hole, but some assistance from the Gemini North telescope also on Mauna Kea finally confirmed its identity: a close-orbiting white dwarf. This complicated the situation. Astronomers previously discovered another white dwarf circling the red dwarf at a much greater distance. Taken altogether, that made three stars existing in a single system. The grouping is now known as Welopō‘ai, a Hawaiian phrase that roughly translates to “path of family traits” in reference to the stars’ shared relationships. According to researchers, no other comparable example can be found within 100 light-years of Earth.

However, Welopō‘ai still doesn’t quite add up. The red dwarf’s nearest companion was about 40 percent more massive than our sun prior to transforming into a white dwarf. When it did, it would have expanded hundreds of times its original size. Previously documented systems featuring these dynamics entailed the two stars falling into an even tighter orbit, or even merging. Despite this, Welopō‘ai’s red dwarf is still there and in a strikingly stable, wide orbit with the closest white dwarf. The team now prepares to continue observing their discovery to learn as much as possible about the triple-star system, and possibly figure out how it formed in the first place.

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” added study co-author and astronomer, Étienne Artigau.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG.

  • Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

It has been revealed that coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios indicates the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

Industry observers note that the game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

According to recent reports, as it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

According to recent reports, though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#132744. The Body Shame Daughters Inherit From the Women They Love

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Body Shame Daughters Inherit From the Women They Love

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • A young girl watches as her mother stands in front of the mirror, sucking in her stomach.
  • According to recent reports, these seemingly ordinary interactions can shape how girls experience their own bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

A young girl watches as her mother stands in front of the mirror, sucking in her stomach. Later, at a family birthday celebration, the girl's grandmother declines a slice of cake, explaining that she has already eaten too much. The girl takes in everything she has seen and heard from two women she loves. Although neither has mentioned anything about the girl's body, the message has been received loud and clear: She has learned that eating requires justification, that weight must be monitored, and that a woman's appearance is something she should continually evaluate.

According to recent reports, these seemingly ordinary interactions can shape how girls experience their own bodies. Over time, these messages become so familiar they feel like personal convictions rather than beliefs learned from others.

According to recent reports, children learn about themselves by observing the people whose affection and approval matter most to them. When a mother expresses dissatisfaction with her appearance, her daughter observes how someone she admires evaluates herself.

Sources indicate that A girl who repeatedly hears her mother criticize her weight may begin to believe that being thin is essential to feeling attractive or acceptable. Even when a mother tells her daughter she is beautiful, her own behavior can send a different message.

Industry observers note that research confirms the influence of these indirect messages. In a study of 50 mothers and their daughters aged 8 to 12 (Handford et al., 2018), girls whose mothers made self-critical comments about their own appearance and dieting reported lower body satisfaction and more problematic eating attitudes than girls whose mothers made no such comments.

In a recent development, the attitudes women pass to their daughters rarely begin with them but instead reflect the cultural messages they absorbed growing up. Despite a major push in recent years to change those messages, they have only changed form.

It has been revealed that for centuries, the consistent message has been that a woman's appearance determines her worth. Restrictive dieting has been praised as discipline and self-control. As each new generation grows up, girls learn to connect appearance with how women are valued.

These messages become embedded in family culture. Comments about gaining weight are treated as expressions of concern. Compliments focus on thinness. Eating certain foods produces guilt, while resisting them earns praise.

According to recent reports, A study of 242 grandmother-mother-daughter groups examined how disordered eating moves across generations (Arroyo et al., 2017). Maternal comments and modeling played key roles in these patterns. Disordered eating did not pass directly through all three generations, but indirect relationships emerged through how women communicated about food and weight.

In a recent development, A more recent study of 634 mothers (Ferrer et al., 2025) found that women who recalled weight-related comments in childhood were more likely to make similar comments to their own children. Those who remembered their parents dieting and commenting on their own weight were also more likely to repeat those behaviors.

Recent findings suggest that these findings help explain why harmful messages sometimes persist within loving families. Messages about appearance become familiar through repetition, and women may pass them along without recognizing their influence. Family history influences later behavior, but it does not determine it. The patterns remain open to change.

Body shame reaches beyond appearance, influencing a woman's sense of worth and how she expects others to perceive her.

According to recent reports, A girl who grows up watching the women around her struggle with their bodies may associate femininity with self-criticism. As she gets older, gaining weight feels like a personal failure. Her confidence comes to depend on how closely her appearance matches an ideal she never consciously chose.

These beliefs are particularly difficult to question when they develop within close family relationships. Children rely on caregivers to help them make sense of themselves and the world, which gives family messages an influence that can last well into adulthood. Eventually, a woman may hear her mother's criticism in her own thoughts. What began as an observation has then become part of her internal dialogue.

It has been revealed that many mothers and grandmothers are responding to expectations they have little power to change. Some genuinely believe that encouraging weight control will protect their daughters from social rejection. Others struggle with their own feelings of inadequacy and have never experienced a different way of relating to their bodies.

In my published clinical work on the intergenerational transmission of trauma (Franco, 2023), I have examined how experiences within one generation influence the emotional lives of those that follow. Body shame has many possible origins, and its presence alone does not establish a history of trauma. Still, family history can show how beliefs become embedded in relationships and persist across generations.

Sources indicate that this perspective also makes room for compassion. Recognizing the harm of inherited messages does not require condemning the women who passed them along. Their intentions, circumstances, and limitations are all part of the story.

According to recent reports, for many women, body shame feels inseparable from identity because it has been present for as long as they can remember. Viewing these beliefs in the context of family relationships and personal history can begin to loosen their hold.

A woman may recognize that the critical voice she experiences when looking in the mirror echoes attitudes she observed throughout childhood. Exploring those connections helps her distinguish what she genuinely believes from what she learned to accept as true.

This awareness creates opportunities for change. Women can begin questioning the assumption that their worth depends on appearance and develop a relationship with food that is less governed by guilt. Mothers who recognize these patterns in themselves can also become more intentional about the messages their daughters receive. This process takes time, particularly when body shame is connected to deeper experiences of rejection or emotional distress.

Sources indicate that the women of previous generations often carried expectations they never had the opportunity to challenge. Recognizing those expectations offers their daughters and granddaughters the possibility of carrying something different forward.

Arroyo, A., Segrin, C., & Andersen, K. K. (2017). Intergenerational transmission of disordered eating: Direct and indirect maternal communication among grandmothers, mothers, and daughters. Body Image, 20, 107–115.

Ferrer, E., Marhan, S., Haller, L., & O'Connor, S. M. (2025). Parent to child intergenerational transmission of direct and indirect weight and shape communication. Journal of Child and Family Studies, 34(8), 2070–2080.

It has been revealed that franco, F. (2023). Intergenerational transmission of trauma. Journal of Health Service Psychology, 49(4), 185–190.

According to recent reports, handford, C. M., Rapee, R. M., & Fardouly, J. (2018). The influence of maternal modeling on body image concerns and eating disturbances in preadolescent girls. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 100, 17–23.
