This $35 leakproof travel mug from BrüMate is for those who don’t mix their coffee with their electronics. A ceramic lining preserves flavor while preventing staining and leftover odors, and triple insulation keeps drinks hot or cold for hours. It’s cup-holder friendly for caffeinating on the go, and a magnetic, OctaLock lid prevents spills while running errands.

The Click & Carry Ergonomic Grocery Bag Carrier Handle & Bag Holder is a $14 gizmo that saves trips and reduces hassle when unloading groceries. It’s gentle on joints, reduces hand strain, and its ergonomic design lowers injury risk. The bag carrier has a 100-pound weight capacity but weighs just under three ounces. The friend who always tests the boundaries of bringing everything inside in one trip will thank you.

Sources indicate that socks are a well-liked practical gift, and this $25 two-pack of merino wool, COOLMAX EcoMade polyester, REPREVE recycled polyester + nylon socks from Gordini uses fine-gauge and ultra-lightweight yarns to keep feet dry and supported with Linear Wicking Channels that move away moisture and Quilted AirForms that distribute shock and cushion impact. These OrbitFit anatomically mapped 3D zones create a purpose-knit performance fit that keeps you comfortable at home, on a walk, or while running or hiking. If cotton socks are on the gift list, we’re fans of the HUE Women’s Mini Crew Sock and the Men’s Casual Ribbed Crew Socks, which are breathable and comfortable.

Sources indicate that the Garmin Venu 4 is a $550 multisport watch that blends style and function. A bright 1.4-inch AMOLED display clearly highlights health and fitness stats like sleep tracking and time needed for workout recovery, along with on-screen workouts. A smart wake alarm helps with waking up at an optimal time, and a built-in LED flashlight illuminates dark morning walks. This watch supports running and triathlon, strength training, jet lag recovery, and more. Data-obsessed friends and family members will be pleased with all the numbers and stats they can pull from this watch.

Industry observers note that this $50 OtterBox Symmetry Series Case has protected my iPhone 13 for years: the only blemish is a dent in the aluminum bumper from when I took it out of its case and immediately dropped it on my concrete porch. I’ve learned my lesson and never forgo a phone case. The OtterBox Symmetry Series Case is sleek without being too flimsy and protects without bulk. It’s on my repurchase list and should be on yours, too, especially if you’re looking at one of the new iPhone 18s.

It has been revealed that these newly refreshed noise-canceling headphones from Bose are essential for quiet commutes and tuning out the airport chaos while traveling. Bose makes some of our favorite noise-canceling headphones and earbuds thanks to thoughtful design and helpful tech in each pair. We’re particularly fond of the comfortable pill-shaped earcups, 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

Sources indicate that this practical gift is also personal. Every pair of these $249 orthotics from Stride is custom-made from a 3D scan of someone’s foot and a gait video with just their smartphone required, no doctor’s visit necessary. Take a short quiz about pain areas, activity levels, goals, and shoe preferences; provide the digital data; and podiatrists in Germany customize the orthotics and print them on durable TPU (personalized for the recipient) before they arrive at your doorstep in just 10 to 15 days. And they go well beyond arch support. It’s hard to convey the initially odd and then swiftly invigorating sensation of an insole that considers each unique contour of the ball of your foot, but we guarantee your achiest friend or family member will appreciate a custom gift that addresses a big pain point, literally.

Recent findings suggest that I hate when gloves hinder my range of movement. These $85 bike gloves from Hestra have a flexible but durable outer fabric and stretchy polyester on the palm. Primaloft Gold synthetic insulation, a fleece lining, and a membrane that stops rain and slush without making hands clammy keep your fingers warm. And the Lycra-clad slit makes the glove easy to put on and take off. Even if we don’t ride, these gloves could be our ride or die.

Industry observers note that style and practicality can go hand-in-hand. The Danner Chelsea boot is just that: Proudly assembled in the organization’s Portland, Oregon factory with signature stitchdown construction, it slips on and is made of full-grain leather. The nonconductive (Electrical Hazard Certified) outsole is oil- and slip-resistant and is comfortable and durable even after climbing on ladders or standing on unforgiving surfaces like wood, tile, or concrete. Even better, the boots are Danner Recraftable, meaning they are eligible for part replacements, leather care, and restitching (paid services), so you are investing in someone’s ongoing comfort. If your gift recipient is good with laces, the Bull Run Moc Toe is another top choice for both looks and stability.

Sources indicate that these $249 Nike slides are a collab with recovery company Hyperice, known for its wellness and recovery technology (we’re currently testing the Normatec dynamic air compression massage legs to positive effect). The comfortable slides combine heat, vibration, and responsive cushioning to make every step feel lighter. They’re like giving a pair of heated slippers a friar-like tonsure.

There’s a woman in your life who carries the world on their shoulders. They shouldn’t have to carry back pain, too. Maybe you’ve heard about Taylor Swift’s posture-correcting bra, or maybe you’ve just listened to a busty friend (or your mom) complain that her back feels like a janky Jenga stack of crooked vertebrae. Is this nearly $200 bra worth it? In a word: absolutely. Designed in seven sizes, up to a G cup, this FDA-registered posture corrector looks like a high-necked crop top with extra-wide straps and a mesh front panel. It gently pulls shoulders into alignment and hugs the girls with serious support—fair warning, though: it can be a wrestling match to get it on and off at first. This one’s more for workouts or lounging at home than for a lift-and-separate situation. Still, it can battle desk-job hunch and is a major relief from digging bra straps.

Know somebody in your family who claims “I’m just a little stiff!” while grimacing as they ease down the stairs after pickleball? Then you know someone who would appreciate the gift of some McDavid support. For instance, the $56.99 NRG above wraps polymer springs on each side of the knee for energy return, while taking up to 12.5 percent stress off each knee. And if that someone you know if coming back from something more serious than soreness, there are slip-on neoprene sleeves for stability all the way to braces that add Maximum+ support, for serious rehab, once you go up to the hinged Bio-Logix line. And once someone is back to throwing their body around, they could appreciate the HEX padded sleeves and compression tights. Brand ambassador Kyrie Irving vouches for them after a torn ACL. And since McDavid has gear that is HSA/FSA-eligible, you can treat yourself to fatigue relief, too, if you’ve got some use-it-or-lose-it dollars left at the end of 2026.

Industry observers note that just because you see a jacket that you feel suits you doesn’t always mean it fits you. The same goes for folks on your gift list. But there’s an alternative to something off-the-rack that’s right in the shoulders but maybe tight in the hips. Maybe the sleeves are right, but it only works if you don’t zip it. Or maybe it’s only available in cost-prohibitive heirloom hides. Well, the Jacket Maker will cut a style to the wearer’s own measurements, and every measurement in their guide comes with a how-to video to make sure you get it right. The team also checks numbers against standard sizing and clarifies/suggests alterations if anything stands out. After that, decisions come down to the customer, from the leather and lining to adding embroidery or emblems, and choosing different shades of hardware. Once completed and pictures are approved, which can take 5-7 weeks, it’s shipped worldwide for free, with duties included at checkout. Sure, gifting at Christmas means they’ll be wearing it in spring, but there’s a thrill in the customization and anticipation and finally seeing them actually reach for that favorite jacket every time they head toward the door. It’ll give you and them a warm, fuzzy feeling … literally, with the right liner. (And there are plentiful ready-to-wear styles, too, if that’s more your jam.).

Sources indicate that the Rode NT1 Signature Series is a $159 workhorse. This cardioid condenser microphone has warm bass, a detailed midrange, and glistening highs for exceptional performance when recording bedroom melodies and harmonies, instruments, voiceovers, and a podcast episode that may never see the sun. Choose from eight vibrant colors, including red, green, blue, cobalt, and orange, or stick with black. Keep us updated on the views and streams! And if you’re looking for an extremely versatile mic and willing to pay a little more, the AKG C114 Large Diaphragm Multi-Pattern Condenser Microphone is a 2026 release we’ve seen used to record an entire band to a greatly immersive effect.

Gifting gear or a gadget related to someone’s hobby will always be a hit. If someone in your life recently got an acoustic guitar, a clip-on tuner is a present that keeps giving. This high-precision tuner blocks room noise for faster, easier tuning. Strummed chords ring out in tune, and songs sound infinitely better for it. If an electric guitar and a pedalboard are part of the gear setup, consider adding a tuner pedal like the TC Electronic POLYTUNE 3.

After many frigid Pittsburgh winters, I’ve learned that investing in a down jacket always pays off. I’m a fan of Stio’s $449 Colter Down Jacket, but the Hometown style is an even more budget-friendly down jacket. A recycled nylon ripstop outer with a PFAS-free DWR shields from the elements. It’s insulated with HyperDRY water-repellent goose down that offers 800-fill warmth even in wet snow. Other helpful features include pockets for hand warmers and valuable tech, and low-profile cord locks for a customized fit. We also think this limited-edition anniversary denim print shown above is just darling.

#132742. I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living.
  • Sources indicate that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work.
  • In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride upcoming e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

Sources indicate that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

According to recent reports, and while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

Sources indicate that this isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

In a recent development, if you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most crucial accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

Industry observers note that for reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

The Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

Industry observers note that the Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

No bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

Recent findings suggest that I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most crucial piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

Industry observers note that I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

It has been revealed that triEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

Sources indicate that as it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

It takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can quickly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

That’s why I’ve become a substantial fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the newly introduced TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

Recent findings suggest that for longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

Despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once quickly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”.

The bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

Recent findings suggest that and for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

According to recent reports, I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

There are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

The reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

Sources indicate that airTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

That’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty promptly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

Sources indicate that I’m a big believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

Sources indicate that it looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

According to recent reports, I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

Sources indicate that of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a big win in my book.

Sources indicate that tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a significant believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

Tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

Recent findings suggest that the Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the crucial bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

Recent findings suggest that this is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

Industry observers note that at $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as major as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

It’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

Industry observers note that I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

According to recent reports, anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

It has been revealed that you can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

The jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

If you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

It has been revealed that it took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

According to recent reports, drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

Sources indicate that the lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

Industry observers note that but now that it’s installed? I love it!

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

The HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

Recent findings suggest that it folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

Sources indicate that just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

That’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

Sources indicate that sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

The Part of Your Holiday Hangover You Can’t See

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that FOUR GLASSES OF wine?
  • In a recent development, the liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more.
  • WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that FOUR GLASSES OF wine? Your liver drinks them, too. Extra gravy? Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together. Nearly every bite you eat and every drink you down ends up getting managed by the same organ in your body: your liver.

In a recent development, the liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more. But come the holidays, all the food and festive drinking can put your body’s largest organ to the test. Here’s how the wreckage happens and how to avoid accumulating long-term damage.

WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale. The liver also holds on to anything it can use, such as the antioxidants in wine or the carbs in beer. But that doesn’t mean alcohol is nutritious. Metabolizing alcohol also creates fatty acids along the way, which get stored as triglycerides—a kind of cholesterol—until your body can use them up. Typically, if you eat and drink moderately, your body processes them just fine. Until you...

THE MORE YOU drink, the more your liver shuffles those triglycerides into the “burn later” pile...until the pile is so substantial that your liver can’t get to the bottom of it.

“If you binge, then binge again, then binge again, your liver gets shocked each time and can’t recover,” says Christopher Koh, MD, clinical director at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

Industry observers note that you may not feel the damage on your liver after the holiday or the next one. But over time, the holidays may overwhelm the organ. This can look like increased inflammation that eventually kills off liver cells, leaving scar tissue in their place (and can lead to cirrhosis, a problem in which 25- to 34-year-olds have the highest risk of death compared with other age groups). Not good. Experts say just three get-togethers a week through the holiday season can initiate inflammation if each outing involves more than five servings of alcohol in two hours. Not to mention when...

In a recent development, YOU DON’T EVEN have to drink alcohol to mess up your liver. Seasonal foods (you know the sides that are delicious but are high in saturated fat or refined carbs, along with processed red meat) combined with holiday-associated weight gain may increase the risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

“It’s estimated that up to 30 percent of the US population has [MASLD], and there aren’t symptoms, so people usually don’t know and aren’t doing anything to reverse it,” notes Mazen Noureddin, MD, hepatologist at Houston Methodist.

In a recent development, as obesity continues to rise, researchers estimate MASLD rates will rise to over 41 percent of the US population in 2050. That fat is wreaking the same havoc alcohol does—causing inflammation and eventual scarring—without the libations. MASLD may develop in as little as six weeks if you really overdo it.

YOU DON’T NEED to buy an activated-charcoal smoothie or a beet-juice detox cleanse to do it. Your liver can regenerate and naturally get itself back in working order if you move the heck out of its way. A month or so without a drop of alcohol (no beer during the game, no wine during date night) can reduce the fat storage in the liver and help tame inflammation. You can also undo some of the fat that causes MASLD by cleaning up your diet and cutting portion sizes: Losing 5 percent of your weight can reduce up to 25 percent of liver fat.

#132739. Industry News: Benevolence, Not Beneficence, Will Drive Trust in AI

Industry News: Benevolence, Not Beneficence, Will Drive Trust in AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • It has been revealed that years ago, I was visiting Notre-Dame in Paris and was moved to light a votive candle, thinking of my young and growing family.
  • Recent findings suggest that coincidentally, the visit came while my coauthors and I were developing our research on consumer trust, and that research showed us that benevolence is key to trust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

It has been revealed that years ago, I was visiting Notre-Dame in Paris and was moved to light a votive candle, thinking of my young and growing family. It also reconnected me to the teaching from my Catholic school, back in Hyderabad, India, and the idea of giving without counting the cost, a phrase from the prayer credited to St. Ignatius.

Recent findings suggest that coincidentally, the visit came while my coauthors and I were developing our research on consumer trust, and that research showed us that benevolence is key to trust. A key dimension in our model, across industries, is operational benevolence, or behavior by a company that reflects a motivation to put the customer’s interest ahead of the provider’s own (Sirdeshmukh, Singh, & Sabol, 2002). When I hear firms building AI describe their purpose in terms of beneficence, a word that sounds much like benevolence but asks far less of a firm, I fear that they are aiming too low and, frankly, not investing in building trust.

According to recent reports, beneficence means doing good and not doing harm. In research ethics, the Belmont Report treats beneficence as an obligation with two rules: do not harm, and maximize possible benefits while minimizing possible harms.

It has been revealed that but in business, that obligation is assumed; you’d not expect to be offering something to the market that does harm, or is even merely neutral in its value. A hospital is expected to act for the good of its patients, and an airline to get its passengers where they are going safely; a firm that failed at this would not stay in business long.

Recent findings suggest that medicine draws the line clearly. The American Medical Association’s Code of Medical Ethics lists a commitment to act for the good of patients among the duties of a trustworthy physician, alongside professional competence. When the Code says what fosters a patient’s trust, however, it points to the physician’s responsibility to place the patient’s welfare above the physician’s own self-interest. Beneficence is necessary; benevolence builds trust.

AI ethics has largely focused on beneficence and neglected benevolence. A review of 84 sets of AI ethics guidelines issued by companies, governments, and research institutions found non-maleficence, the principle of avoiding harm, in 60 of them and beneficence in about half (Jobin, Ienca, & Vayena, 2019). Benevolence did not appear among the 11 principles the reviewers identified.

When an AI firm presents beneficence as its purpose, it is in effect describing the work of training a system that could go wrong to do good instead. While that improvement may feel substantial to the people doing that work, correcting something that could go bad is not an achievement a firm should want to tout, let alone make the great purpose of the company. It is the floor that customers, regulators, and the public already expect.

Industry observers note that geoffrey Hinton’s suggestion that AI be built with maternal instincts, to me, reads as him saying that AI should have benevolence coded into it. Maternal instinct is more than caring. A mother will do what it takes for her child, at a cost to herself, and that is a different thing from doing good. The promise of going to any extent to protect the welfare of the child is why the maternal posture is held up as a driver of trust, and even faith.

If AI firms mean trustworthiness and trust, then what they are taking on is a much heavier burden, and that is benevolence. When we were developing our model of trust, our interviews, focus groups, and then survey all showed something similar. Customers saw actions that showed that the firm put their interests ahead of (or at least in line with) the firm’s interests as central to trustworthiness. Benevolence, more than competence, drove trust and loyalty in a majority of our studies.

The burden lies in the cost. Benevolence almost always means that a provider has taken on a cost, is taking on a cost, or is willing to take one on. For a firm, this is what giving without counting the cost means. When it bears a cost it was not required to bear, customers can infer something about its intentions. Economists make a related point about signaling: a signal is credible when it would be too costly to send for someone who lacks the quality it claims (Spence, 1973).

It has been revealed that in AI, the costs are easy to name: delaying a release until a model is shown to be safe, declining a business model built on capturing users’ attention, holding back a capability until those who defend against its misuse have it, and disclosing a model’s weaknesses along with its strengths. Even a large language model that, in its chat, risks user unhappiness and disengagement by offering advice that, on its face, may be seen as negative, is taking a benevolent action.

When customers or patients come to recognize that a provider is benevolent, that is where trust really occurs. It is also what Hinton’s image of the mother conveys: protective, concerned, vigilant, and willing to sacrifice, and trusted for that reason. AI firms that want to be trusted in the same way will have to show, over time and at some cost to themselves, that they will do right by their users when the two sets of interests diverge. Ironically, just showing the intent to do good is a low threshold for trust.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks.
  • According to recent reports, by far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a fresh electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

Designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I said tracks.

According to recent reports, by far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most massive material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

The Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

Mantsinen says its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

Recent findings suggest that mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The firm claims HybriLift improves the major machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

Industry observers note that and, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is presently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

What do you guys think – is this massive material handler the thing you need for your logging or scrapyard, or are you holding out for something even bigger? Let us know in the comments.

The first phase of Luna 3 will feature Durin and Jahoda, alongside the return of Venti. The second phase sees no new character debuts, but does feature the return of Varesa and Xilonen.

There’s more to get excited about in Luna 3, even if you don’t feel like spending most of your time in Nod-Krai. The Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey event will take you back to Dragonspine, where you’ll find winter-theme minigames appropriate to an revision cycle spanning December to January. This is how you can earn the 4-Star Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, so, you think you can run an electric car company? Well, here’s your chance to prove it. An entire electric vehicle development project is heading to auction this month, and it comes with almost everything you need to get started. There's even a connection to one of the automotive industry's most beloved defunct brands: Saab.

As first brought to our attention by Great Britain’s Car, Swedish auction company Klaravik is preparing to sell the entire NEVS Emily GT project. The auction includes four complete prototype vehicles, a fifth development mule, spare body panels, parts, tools, and engineering drawings. And unlike a typical automotive auction, where you might leave with a single vehicle, the winning bidder gets the entire collection.

A little backstory is helpful here. After Saab Automobile closed its doors in 2012 following an ill-fated tie-up with Spyker, a Chinese consortium called National Electric Vehicle Sweden (NEVS) acquired the majority of the remaining assets, including the Trollhättan factory, manufacturing equipment and intellectual property. However, NEVS was not interested in building a next-generation Saab 9-3 Aero. Instead, they had their sights set on building an electric car future.

Their vision of that was called the Emily GT, envisioned as a sophisticated electric grand touring sedan capable of competing with established luxury EVs. Development began in late 2019, and just 10 months later, the Emily GT rolled out into view. And much like Saabs of the past, the Emily GT had some unique features—the most obvious being its four electric motors, one mounted inside each wheel. Combined, they produced a healthy 490 horsepower.

It has been revealed that however, while the power output was healthy, the financial condition of the company was not. NEVS never secured the funding necessary to bring the car into production. The ambitious project remained stuck in the prototype stage, where it’s stayed frozen .

Sources indicate that so, do you think you’re the right person to bring it to market? If so—or even if you’d rather just own a very odd automotive dead-end—Klaravik will open online bidding on November 25, with the auction scheduled to conclude December 9. All four completed vehicles and the accompanying development materials are being offered together rather than individually.

Industry observers note that of course, buying the prototypes and engineering materials doesn't automatically give someone a functioning car tech giant or guarantee a path to production. Manufacturing, regulatory approvals, and financing would still present enormous challenges. However, if you do happen to be an ambitious entrepreneur with deep pockets, this could be your chance to revive an electric vehicle that never had the chance to see the light of day.

How to use your phone if the grid goes down

💡 Key Takeaways

  • There are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down? Power and tech outages continue to cause disruptions, and that can leave you stuck when it comes to staying in touch with others.

There are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it. You’ll need to make sure the people you’re chatting with have set up the same options, so it’s worth mentioning at the next family or friends gathering.

Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.

It has been revealed that if you’ve acquired a phone from Apple, Samsung, or Google in the last two or three years, it comes with satellite communications built in, so you can still text friends and family if the cell towers go out (calling isn’t an option, due to bandwidth). The feature should kick in automatically in Messages on iOS, or in Google Messages on Android, provided your carrier supports it—you’ll just see a prompt on screen.

Follow the instructions to find a satellite and start texting. There’s nothing to enable or turn on, but if you want to test it out beforehand so you know it works, open Settings, then pick Apps > Messages > Satellite Connection Demo (iOS), or Safety and emergency > Satellite SOS (Android).

There is another option on your phone, which is to try a peer-to-peer messaging app. These apps need to be downloaded in advance and work over Bluetooth to send messages in a mesh created by the devices themselves. That means a limited range, but you don’t need any Wi-Fi or cellular connectivity.

Sources indicate that one of the best apps in this category is Bridgefy, which you can get for Android and iOS. It’s free to use, simple to operate, and has a range of around 100 meters (or 330 feet). You don’t have to wait until the power goes out to use it either, because you could set up a mesh chat when you’re out camping or taking a trip with family.

Unless you do a lot of outdoor, off-grid adventuring, you might not have realized just how many devices now exist that can keep you connected even without access to Wi-Fi or cellular networks. Some of these options work via the same satellite networks as your phone.

Sources indicate that have a look at the Garmin InReach Messenger Plus, for example, a $299.99 communicator you can use whenever cell networks are down (or just out of range). You’re also going to need an active subscription. They start at $7.99 a month, but once you’re set up you can connect to the wider world from just about anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that then there are the more straightforward walkie-talkie devices, which operate over radio signals across a range of a few miles. That might just be enough if you’ve got friends and family you need to contact when the power’s out. There are plenty of devices to choose between, but the Motorola T802 Talkabout is a good example and under $100 for a pair.

Industry observers note that don’t forget a battery-powered radio either. It won’t let you message anyone directly, but it will mean you can stay up to date with what’s happening out there in the world, and it might give you an idea of when the power’s going to come back on. You can even get models that work via solar or hand-crank power, like this $30 emergency radio.

Recent findings suggest that all of your phones and other devices will need power if they’re going to keep you in touch with other people—otherwise you’ll be relying on smoke signals and postal couriers. So it’s wise to invest in a portable power station ahead of time. Something like the $289 Jackery Explorer 300 would do the job.

Obviously, you’re going to want to charge up these hefty power stations before the electricity gets cut, otherwise they won’t be much use. But you’re actually not as reliant on the power grid as you might think. Many models (including those offered by Jackery) have solar panel add-ons you can invest in as well.

According to recent reports, even with a backup supply in place, it’s a good idea to try and conserve power on your gadgets as much as possible too. Your phones, tablets, and laptops will all have low power settings you can make use of, but there are standard tips that apply across just about every gadget. Reduce screen brightness and volume as much as possible, and enable airplane mode where you can.

According to recent reports, when you do have power and Wi-Fi available, make sure you download as much essential info to your phone as you can, so it’s still there when an internet connection isn’t. This is particularly useful for maps: Both Google Maps (Settings > Offline maps) and Apple Maps (Profile picture > Offline maps) let you do this.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, toyota is getting into electric bikes.
  • The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.
  • According to recent reports, and when Toyota claims compact, it means it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

According to recent reports, and when Toyota claims compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the firm is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

Toyota calls the latest Scion a “freedom lab” where the organization can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota revealed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

According to recent reports, and I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota indicates the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

Toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

It has been revealed that believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota notes his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t declared production plans or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota says a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

I’m obviously a major believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

Sources indicate that but hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

#132731. What a Cardboard Titanic Taught Me About Children and AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

What a Cardboard Titanic Taught Me About Children and AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • I once had a student who found reading extremely difficult.
  • According to recent reports, he painted the entire thing in the same black and red colors as the real ship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

I once had a student who found reading extremely difficult. Phonemic awareness didn’t come easily. With reading, he needed a lot of adult support. On the other hand, he was able to build a massive, two-meter-long cardboard model of the Titanic with every detail: the smokestacks, the lifeboats, the captain’s quarters with a ship’s wheel, and even a wooden popsicle stick deck.

According to recent reports, he painted the entire thing in the same black and red colors as the real ship. His fine motor skills were exceptional, and he worked through iterations, changing, building, and rebuilding over the course of two months. If the popsicle sticks didn’t attach the right way, he built a cardboard scaffold underneath. When he wanted the lifeboats to hang, he tried different ways before settling on pipe cleaners. This wasn’t part of a history project. He was just doing it during his self-directed learning time, completely by himself. So, what does this story say about executive functioning?

Sources indicate that his struggles in class and his well-developed design thinking skills seem to point in opposite directions, but that’s only true if we define executive functioning as a single trait that you either have more or less of. In this child, we see it full throttle in one kind of work and not another, which is why I believe it should be viewed more like a capability that grows through use, rather than a deficit. It’s actually still growing, even if not through reading, in this case. Adele Diamond and Daphne Ling reviewed the research on programs that claim to improve executive function and found that these skills improve through practice and carry over to tasks needing similar skills. The strongest gains come from activities we care about.

Sources indicate that around the same time he was building that ship, I was outside at the four square courts listening to an episode of Conversations With Tyler hosting developmental scientist Alison Gopnik, who was describing the way young children learn. “Rational Bayesians," as she called the children, run small experiments on the world and change what they believe based on what actually happens. In some respects, she claims, they do it better than scientists. Every version of a lifeboat that he tried or a smokestack that didn’t hold the cotton smoke properly—and every rebuild that followed—was one of those experiments. So what happens if we stick technology, AI, or a screen in front of this child at this moment?

Presumably, an AI tool could also have designed a plan, the structure, and the steps for building the Titanic. Yet, isn't that exactly where Diamond and Ling say executive functioning is getting built through practice and effort?

This has always been my concern when we view AI as a technological support when it risks crowding out the active, self-directed practice that builds problem-solving and executive function. Back in 2011, Elizabeth Bonawitz conducted an experiment where an adult demonstrated to a preschooler one thing a newly introduced toy could do. As a result, those children explored the toy less and found fewer of its other functions than children who weren’t shown and got to work it out alone. When the children were given the answer up front, they rationally assumed the search was over.

Gopnik’s lab also looked at the difference between children’s brains and machines in a 2023 study in which 4-year-olds started exploring how a machine functioned by working it out themselves. When the same evidence was described in words to language models, the models couldn’t find the rules. The authors' reading is that these systems are very good at passing along what people already know, and much less able to discover something latest. The models they tested were much less sophisticated than the ones today, but the distinction drawn between imitation and innovation is something I routinely run across in my classroom. AI tools can imitate brilliantly, but a child's invention comes from variance, from trying something that wasn’t suggested.

Handing students AI-generated aims treats every open-ended problem as if there is some magical, single “correct” template, which consequently cuts off the messy variance, the diverse beauty, we’ve come to expect from children in our classrooms. Our students are now growing up beside this fresh technology, this new imitation of intelligence, that will demonstrate the function of anything, instantly, on request. Having this level of assistance at their fingertips suggests that producing something, whether that be an essay, homework, or a summary of The Grapes of Wrath, gets cheaper and easier to do.

According to recent reports, is this a bad thing? I’m not sure; the jury is still out. Regardless, the part that I’m 100 percent confident will remain valuable is the part the child will always be responsible for: the invention, the personal struggle, and the thinking being built behind it. The thinking that builds the Titanic.

I wish I could claim credit; perhaps that I had somehow instructed him to do this as part of a project. The only thing I really did was say “yes.” His reading has improved too, though not because the sounds suddenly clicked in the traditional sense. We adapted a strategy so he builds words by piecing the sounds together in a physical puzzle, much like the way he built the Titanic.

In both cases, the answer was never handed to him. What he received was a way to discover the connections by himself. That search is what a school day has to protect before any technology interferes with that self-discovery.

Conclusions about interventions, programs, and approaches for improving executive functions that appear justified and those that, despite much hype, do not. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that boston’s Upcoming England Aquarium recently shipped a very key package.
  • “By working together, we are able to raise more fish, and develop aquaculture practices to successfully raise more species, including some that have never been raised before, like copper/glassy sweepers, blue chromis, and brown chromis,” Monika Schmück, manager of sustainability in the fishes department at the Fresh England Aquarium, tells Popular Science.
  • According to recent reports, sharing is caring, even amongst aquariums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that boston’s Upcoming England Aquarium recently shipped a very key package. But it wasn’t exactly an early Christmas gift. The team shipped 22 lookdown fish across the country via air transport. And they’re not the only institution that routinely packs fishes up and sends them elsewhere. The NEA are part of a group of aquariums where each member specializes in raising certain species on behalf of the entire group. They then send the fish to the other member aquariums.

“By working together, we are able to raise more fish, and develop aquaculture practices to successfully raise more species, including some that have never been raised before, like copper/glassy sweepers, blue chromis, and brown chromis,” Monika Schmück, manager of sustainability in the fishes department at the Fresh England Aquarium, tells Popular Science. “We typically raise 500-1000 fish annually and distribute them to over 15 institutions on average each year.”.

According to recent reports, sharing is caring, even amongst aquariums. When it comes time for the fish’s journey, the team needs to decide whether to use air or ground transport. To do this, they consider factors including external temperature, the weight of the shipment, and access to an airport at the destination. Depending on the time of the year, cargo holding and ground transport trucks can experience extreme temperatures, Schmück points out.

Recent findings suggest that if it’s a large shipment, the Fresh England Aquarium usually goes for air cargo, whereas smaller shipments are easier to deliver with ground transportation. Overall, ground transportation is the easiest strategy because it doesn’t have to take into account the location of airports.

On a smaller scale, moving a fish isn’t as easy as sticking a cat into a crate. In terms of the container in which the animal will travel, the biggest consideration is the size of said animal, which determines how much water it needs.

“Since fish must be transported in water, and water is heavy, the design of a fish transport first must address how to safely move the required volume of water to keep the fish safe and secure during the process,” Schmück explains.

Ultimately, the fundamentals of fish transport are mostly consistent no matter the species. Experts need to make sure that the water chemistry is good during the entire trip and that other environmental conditions are appropriate for the traveling species and remain stable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.

Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.

Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now released, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.

The recent Black Ops 7 launch clearly hasn’t made many people happy, so just like Activision made Black Ops 6 free to play at BF6’s launch, EA has now done the same with its own game. The Battlefield 6 free trial, which was revealed last week, is just an hour away at the time of this writing.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy launched, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

It has been revealed that the trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

In a recent development, players will have access to four game modes, played on different versions of the same maps. Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch will all be available to choose from, and there don’t appear to be any level or XP limits in the trial.

Unfortunatley, just as the free trial was about to go live, the game got hit with a major matchmaking outage that took down all matchmaking in the core game, leaving Redsec unaffected.

Hopefully EA can resolve this concern before the trial officially kicks off.

#132727. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1369 w)
