  • Sources indicate that I’m standing in front of the fish counter at Market Basket, the grocery store chain that serves much of eastern Massachusetts.
  • Why do we try so hard, at this time of the year, to recreate the recipes from our past?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Sources indicate that I’m standing in front of the fish counter at Market Basket, the grocery store chain that serves much of eastern Massachusetts. I scan the cooler for oysters. Shucked oysters, to be specific. It’s the day before Thanksgiving. I’m trying to recreate the menu of my youth. Those offerings included scalloped oysters, a recipe that my mother made every Thanksgiving and Christmas. Mom passed away in 2023. She never wrote down the recipe. She always followed the "handful of this" and a "pinch of that" school of cooking. She was masterful. I, on the other hand, celebrate the occasional culinary win, but more often than not, my successes are hit or miss—especially when it comes to the infrequent concocting of scalloped oysters.

Why do we try so hard, at this time of the year, to recreate the recipes from our past?

We are attempting to do more than recreate those dishes; we are trying to conjure the ghosts of those friends and family members who are no longer with us.

It has been revealed that roast the perfect turkey. Prepare the perfect pumpkin pie. Arrange an artistic nut tray. Make the perfect mashed potatoes with just enough lumps to know they’re homemade, but not so many that we ask, “Who cooked the potatoes?”.

Sources indicate that some families carefully divvy the work among invited dinner guests. Auntie will handle the fresh cranberry relish, while Cousin brings the almond green bean casserole. Somehow, two people end up making the candied sweet potatoes, but one looks a little gray while the other is adorned with perfectly toasted mini-marshmallows. We will struggle to consume both. We don’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings.

Sources indicate that are we attempting to make Instagram-worthy dishes for the social media kudos? Or are we endeavoring to improve upon the butter-laden, sugary dishes of our youth? Remember that Uncle Robbie needs to watch his caloric intake after suffering a minor heart attack last spring. And Cousin Joanne is supposed to be watching her sugar since she started taking insulin to control her diabetes.

“It’s just one day,” we counter. “How bad could it be?”.

Sources indicate that but there are ethical considerations, too. Shannon’s upcoming friend is vegan. Out of respect, we throw together a dairy-free lasagna. Is that really enough?

Industry observers note that in-laws bring newly introduced traditions. My husband’s grandmother’s family favorite of orange ice befuddles our daughter-in-law’s family, but they agree to serve it every year. “We eat this first?” one asks. “But won’t the turkey get cold?” A question I’ve asked myself for almost fifty years. “Maybe this would be better served for the 4th of July!” someone claims. And we all nod. And we never actually follow through.

Industry observers note that fresh Orleanian author Amy Cyrex Sins mourned the absence of a recipe for Doberge cake after losing her treasured recipe file and her home after Hurricane Katrina ravaged Louisiana in August of 2005. While she suffered the obvious loss of possessions, it was the inability to recreate a favored family treat that continued to jab at her with the sharp barbs of loss, both physical and emotional. I remember sharing her essay with an honors college class many years ago. One student took it upon herself to make the dish. We New Englanders had no context to judge her success, but I know that I enjoyed a slice of cake that day. And I’ll never forget how she cut the cake by carving out a center circle and then cutting slices from the outside rim. A new tradition? Probably not. A new taste memory? Definitely.

But tasting our past and our memories encompasses so much more than carefully measuring and mixing ingredients.

When we attempt to recreate recipes from our childhoods and our pasts, we honor those cooks and chefs of our ancestors.

In a recent development, vera, my maternal grandmother, was a terrible cook. I remember her making hamburgers and boiled potatoes. The patties were overcooked, the potatoes fork-mashed with butter and pepper. That was a staple meal served almost every night of the week! Grammy was a single mother, having been widowed at the age of nineteen. At the time, she was pregnant and had a two-year-old. Survival was critical. Tastes were secondary. And this was during the Great Depression.

One forgives a lack of herbs and spices when cheap ground beef and farm-raised spuds were often rationed between the extended family members of Canadian immigrants.

It has been revealed that psychotherapist and Relationship Expert Mary Pender Greene writes, “Remember that there are NO perfect holidays” (2009, p. 26). She suggests that the malaise of the holidays stems from “unrealistic expectations, which is often inspired by holiday marketing” (Greene, 2009, p. 29). Thank you, Martha Stewart.

One year, my husband received a 24-pound turkey as a bonus from his company. I calculated that the bird would take about 8 hours to roast. Just after 6 a.m., I popped the pale, featherless carcass into the oven. But at about 1 p.m., the fire alarm started to beep. Smoke filled the kitchen. I opened the oven door and orange flames licked at the stove front. My husband doused the fire with the white foam from a trusty fire extinguisher.

We didn’t have turkey that day. We had hamburgers. I think my elderly grandmother actually preferred the Thanksgiving dinner that day.

Industry observers note that this year, I will once again attempt to make my mother’s scalloped oysters. I will be the only one eating them, as my husband and daughter eschew eating shellfish. But that just means more for me.

I hope that I swerve closer to the perfect scalloped oysters of my memories, but even if I miss that mark, I know that I continue to honor a long-held family tradition.

It has been revealed that we strive to taste the memories of the past, but tastes do change. Ingredients become hard to find and obsolete. And that’s absolutely okay.

Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification.
  • UPGRADE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.
  • In a recent development, “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

UPGRADE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

In a recent development, “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”.

Recent findings suggest that pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any newly introduced ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

It has been revealed that when you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

In a recent development, country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

Industry observers note that what’s more, a new wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

With only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

Unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

If disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

In a recent development, if you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

Industry observers note that it’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

Industry observers note that at the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

Industry observers note that and while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some upcoming, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

According to recent reports, I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility company to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

According to recent reports, that said, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

How a red wolf gets a checkup

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Annual human checkups are relatively straightforward.
  • In a recent development, we’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam.
  • “The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Annual human checkups are relatively straightforward. You hop onto the exam table, stick your tongue out, stare straight ahead as the doctor beams light into your eyes, let them tap their small hammer against that wildly uncomfortable spot under your kneecap, etc. But for wildlife, it’s a whole other experience.

In a recent development, we’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam. But what about another favorite carnivore—wolves? According to Vicki Scharfberg, from Roger Williams Park Zoo & Carousel Village in Rhode Island, the annual wellness examination for red wolves (Canis rufus) is not that different from a pet dog’s annual veterinary visit.

“The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.

According to recent reports, the checkup includes a physical examination at the wolf enclosure or the zoo veterinary hospital, bloodwork, vaccinations, heartworm prevention care, and if necessary, parasite treatment. A social media post by Roger Williams Park Zoo showcases their red wolf named Frye thoroughly knocked out on the exam table, undergoing an oral exam, among other things.

According to recent reports, the team uses the bloodwork to check on the wolf’s organs and screen for heartworm disease. Interestingly, their vaccines are the exact same ones veterinarians give to domestic dogs for rabies, distemper, parvovirus, and leptospirosis.

Heartworm prevention treatment involves a long-acting 12 month injection. Heartworm disease is caused by grossly long worms called heartworms that take up residence in an animals’ heart, lungs, and related blood vessels. This parasitic condition triggers severe lung disease, heart failure, and damages other organs. Heartworm is potentially fatal, and in addition to wolves can also impact animals including dogs, cats, ferrets, foxes, and humans.

“If something abnormal is found on the examination, we follow up with additional diagnostics like x-rays, ultrasound, or a consult with a veterinary specialist (dentist, cardiologist, etc),” Scharfberg concludes.

#132703. Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (945 w)

Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off.
  • In a recent development, “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline.
  • Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

In a recent development, “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”.

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, said Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

According to recent reports, “[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

It has been revealed that “It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” remarked Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”.

Bitner remarked women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she said. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”.

In fact, Bitner said providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart plans to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she noted.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

Industry observers note that “My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she remarked. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”.

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical company Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”.

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart mentioned.

In everyday life, Bitner noted that while some patients avoid talking about midlife complications like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

As more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” mentioned Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her glitch because we know it’s not.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s not too often we get latest recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days.
  • The reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda says this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall.
  • Recent findings suggest that honda notes that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material.

Sources indicate that it’s not too often we get latest recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Honda is recalling 16,387 S2000 roadsters from the 2004–20005 model years, the first two years of the AP2 refresh. A quick look at the sales figures for those years seems to suggest that means all (or close to all) S2000s from those years are part of the recall population.

The reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda says this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall. The problem with manufacturing relates to whether or not it was built with brazing material at the joint-to-flange connection. With the part being a push-to-fit part, Honda says this lack of material could cause the connection to become loose and separate.

Recent findings suggest that honda notes that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material. These parts were shipped and potentially installed in S2000s. Honda estimates the percentage of cars with the defect is 1 percent. There won’t be many warning signs before it’s too late to continue driving, but Honda says stalling, a misfire, fuel odor and an inability to start the engine are all symptoms.

It has been revealed that as of now, Honda says there are no injuries or deaths related to this issue. Those with cars in the recall range will have to bring their convertibles into the Honda dealer for the remedy. Once there, it will receive a new and improved fuel flange joint assembly free of charge.

#132699. Conformity, Individuality, and the Lawns of Levittown

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (496 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Conformity, Individuality, and the Lawns of Levittown

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just a few miles from my home is historic Levittown, Long Island, where immediately after WWII, 4,000 acres of potato fields were plowed under to mass-produce more than 17,000 detached houses; many of these four-and-a-half-room homes were constructed in about two days.
  • Selling for less than $8,000 ($115,000 in 2024 dollars), each house came with a TV set and hi-fi.
  • A popular folksong tagged Levittown and other such developments as places of little boxes “made out of ticky tacky/And they all look the same.” No longer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Just a few miles from my home is historic Levittown, Long Island, where immediately after WWII, 4,000 acres of potato fields were plowed under to mass-produce more than 17,000 detached houses; many of these four-and-a-half-room homes were constructed in about two days.

Selling for less than $8,000 ($115,000 in 2024 dollars), each house came with a TV set and hi-fi. Buyers could choose a red, yellow, or blue house in one of three styles, in neighborhoods largely devoid of trees. This first modern suburb prompted historian Lewis Mumford to describe Levittown as “a uniform environment from which escape is impossible.”.

A popular folksong tagged Levittown and other such developments as places of little boxes “made out of ticky tacky/And they all look the same.” No longer.

Sources indicate that drive through the area today, and it is nearly impossible to imagine the architectural conformity that it once was. What is striking about Levittown is that as houses aged, they became distinctive from one another and went decidedly upscale. They expanded upward and sideways. These four-and-a-half-room homes now are four- or five-bedroom houses with two baths. Barren landscapes are long gone. In 2024, Levittown houses were listed in the $700,000 range.

According to recent reports, the sterile 1950s transformed into the turbulent '60s, with subsequent decades bringing tremendous social change in their wake. New generations moved in with new ideas; they had more money than did the returning war veterans. With time, Levittown’s appearance reflected the tastes of new homeowners.

Levittown reflects two contradictory impulses in human nature: The individuality impulse on the one hand, and conformity on the other. It is the universal desire to be recognized as a unique individual but at the same time desiring to be part of a group. The distinctiveness of the home displays this while adhering to the idealized standard of a suburban front lawn. You can drive for miles through Levittown—and almost every suburban neighborhood—and find that while the houses are no longer alike, not a single house has dispensed with grass lawns.

In a recent development, this would be a landscaping choice if it didn’t also mean that, to maintain the carpet-like appearance, the air is polluted with the fumes of mowers, the groundwater is poisoned with fertilizers (Long Island depends exclusively on its aquifer for its drinking water), and a din created by leaf blowers makes a quiet summer day around the house a rare event. Dispensing with lawns will probably have to be a policy decision, as there is only so much individuality that a person can express without feeling like an outsider. The change will have to come as an imposed municipal edict; not having a manicured lawn becomes a new enforced norm, where conformity becomes not having a grassy lawn.

As a red wave of Chinese-built electric vehicles breaks over Europe and Canada, Xiaomi is selling its electric cars outside of China for the first time ever – and its starting its push for global growth with the UAE in 2027.

According to recent reports, xiaomi is selling its electrified vehicles to buyers outside of China for first time this week, with the SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover, and Skynomad SUV now listed for sale throughout the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The organization isn’t going it alone, however.

Xiomi is working local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, rather than operating its own retail network, with Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirming that the company would officially enter Western car markets next year at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen held 17NOV.

CarNewsChina reports that Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants across the Xiaomi SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV, and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup, with retail prices starting at 169,900 AED ($~46,200 US) for the SU7 Standard and climbing all the way up to 375,900 AED ($~102,000 US) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra.

Not to lump a bunch of nations with their own rich heritage and car culture together, but it’s fair to say that drivers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait love their supercars – and the brand’s Xiaomi SU7 Ultra might be one of the most super of them all, thanks to fully 1,548 hp from three high-torque electric motors, the SU7 Ultra can sprint from 0-100 km/h (62 mph) in under two seconds on its way to a towering, 217 mph top speed.

It’s not just a straight-line speed machine, either. Xiaomi gave its go-fast flagship a serious track-focused makeover on its way to becomig the “Utlra,” complete with carbon-ceramic brakes, an aggressive (if controversial) composite aero package, an enormous rear wing, and a chassis tuned to tackle the turns the Green Hell of the Nürburgring.

And, at a relatively reasonable $102,000 equivalent price, I’d be willing to bet that a lot of the hypercar-loving Emiratis will be eager to get their hands on one.

The first customer deliveries of the Xiaomi SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro models are scheduled for December of this year, with deliveries of the remaining variants scheduled for February 2027.

#132696. Breaking: Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (963 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • Industry observers note that that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • Many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

Industry observers note that that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

Many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

There’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks reveals that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

Sources indicate that so bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

“They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

According to recent reports, which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

You might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

Industry observers note that if you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

There’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

Recent findings suggest that squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

In a recent development, they are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University showed this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

It has been revealed that the results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

Industry observers note that other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

The Failure Rate of Public Schools Is a Tragedy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • As described in the article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” teenager Najya Hannah-Jones confronted her mother, the prominent journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, about the choice to send her to public school in a system that, for many, provides substandard education.
  • Every parent has a duty to nurture their children, but all parents also must consider their values when choosing schools for their children, so it is heartbreaking to realize that Ms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

As described in the article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” teenager Najya Hannah-Jones confronted her mother, the prominent journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, about the choice to send her to public school in a system that, for many, provides substandard education. It was refreshing to read of Najya fighting to get a better education, a striking contrast with the popular but often inaccurate stereotype of lazy teens aiming to learn as little as possible. More importantly, kudos to Nikole Hannah-Jones for candidly admitting in her article that teachers lied to her about what they were teaching and, worse, tried to deceive both mother and daughter about what had actually been learned.

Every parent has a duty to nurture their children, but all parents also must consider their values when choosing schools for their children, so it is heartbreaking to realize that Ms. Hannah-Jones could have chosen a far better public school in Upcoming York for her daughter that would have met the core values listed in her article. Public school? Check. Racially diverse or perhaps even predominately Black student body? Check. Most importantly, a track record of meeting educational standards and being honest with parents regarding what their child is learning and how they are performing? Check and check.

The truth is that Nikole Hannah-Jones could have enrolled her daughter in a local public school where the majority of students are Black and other nonwhite families and has long offered much better odds for positive educational outcomes. There has long been such an option available to parents that is too often ignored: Fresh York City charter schools.

In the book Charter Schools and Their Enemies, Thomas Sowell painstakingly and convincingly reveals that public charter schools in New York City consistently outperform neighborhood schools. Based on Ms. Hannah-Jones essay, one could argue that is not an especially high bar, but the data in the book show academic superiority relative to even the higher-quality schools in New York City, New York State, and nationwide. It is noteworthy that Sowell meticulously controls for the usual “straw men” used to assault charter schools. Indeed, some of the charter schools were not only in the same neighborhoods, but in the same building as the comparison schools in his study.

It is an ongoing tragedy that Ms. Hannah-Jones and others in the Black community are not demanding an expansion of public charter school options for their children. After all, and perhaps this is why they are under assault, public charter schools provide prima facia evidence that Fresh York can, in fact, deliver a high-quality public education, but chooses not to do so. One hopes that other families like the Hannah-Joneses will enroll their children in public charter schools and demand that New York City be more honest what is being taught and what their children have learned.

In a recent development, the national discussion Ms. Hannah-Jones has sparked has been overwhelmingly focused on schools with majority Black student enrollment, but the debate should not be narrowly circumscribed. The truth is that every teen enrolled in failing schools across the U.S. should be asking their parents the same question Najya Hannah-Jones asked her mother: Why are you sending me to a school you already know is delivering a substandard education?

Stripped to essentials, Ms. Hannah-Jones faced the same choice most families do when deciding whether to enroll their children in public schools, regardless of race: If I send my child to the local school as a kindergartner, what is the probability that my child will emerge from 8th grade with the basic reading and math skills needed to succeed in high school and beyond? It turns out that there are ample data to help parents answer this question.

In a recent development, the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) provides annual statistics on U.S. education outcomes. Nationally, only 26% of 8th-graders are proficient or above in math, according to its 2022 Nation's Report Card; only about one in four children are entering high school with grade-level proficiency in math. Reading outcomes are only slightly better, with 28% of 8th-graders being rated as proficient. Candidly, this is a national disgrace that poses an excruciating dilemma for parents and students.

A usual response to this data is to argue that public schools are underfunded. New York spends an average of more than $30,000 per student. Overall, the U.S. consistently spends more per pupil than nearly every other country in the world, including many that deliver better outcomes while paying less than half of what the U.S spends. More money is not translating to better outcomes. Does anyone believe that even doubling expenditures or even tripling them would appreciably improve outcomes at the school Najya Hannah-Jones attended, or any other failing school? After all, real spending, even adjusted for inflation, has more than doubled in the past 25 years and outcomes are actually a bit worse nationwide over the same period.

Recent findings suggest that if it is not simply spending more money, what should parents do? The best answer: Do your homework. There are often options. Many states have adopted public options, including public charter schools, public magnet schools, and other similar approaches.

Sources indicate that several of my own children attended a public school implementing a Montessori teaching approach and two of my granddaughters are presently enrolled in a similar public school in Nashville. I was (and am) very pleased with what they were taught, how they were taught, and what they learned. Another daughter attended an academic magnet public high school that consistently outperforms even the most expensive private schools, even though, in general, Nashville public schools often have relatively poor outcomes for most students. The evidence is overwhelming that public school systems know how to deliver a high-quality education. Why are they choosing not to? Najya Hannah-Jones is absolutely right to demand answers and all teens—and their parents—should be asking the same questions.

Sowell, T. (2020). Charter schools and their enemies. Basic Books.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow, after all these years, there are still a considerable number of vehicles equipped with Takata airbags, though their number should be considerably lower in the near future. Honda just issued a recall for 810,592 cars equipped with Takata airbags that could rupture due to propellant degradation caused by high humidity.

According to documents filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall covers some 2013 Acura RDX, ILX, Honda CR-V, Civic, and Accord models. The affected Accords and Acuras are all from the 2013 model year, while the CR-V and Civic populations include both 2012 and 2013 vehicles.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

It has been revealed that the NHTSA documents show that the affected vehicles are equipped with airbag inflators that use a phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate propellant, which is intended to control moisture within the inflator. Over time, exposure to high humidity and repeated temperature changes can cause the inflator to become brittle. When the brittle inflators are deployed, they could turn into projectiles that shoot metal fragments through the cabin, potentially injuring or killing occupants.

The recall comes after years of investigation and analysis by Honda, which was routinely shared with NHTSA. The recall documents show that on November 19, 2026, Honda determined that the inflators posed enough of a risk to warrant the new recall.

In a recent development, owners of affected models will be contacted by mail and urged to bring their vehicle to a Honda or Acura dealership. Dealer technicians will replace the driver and passenger airbag inflators with a different model for free. Dealers have already been notified of the recall, with owner notification letters scheduled to be sent on December 18. Owners concerned that their car might be included in the recall can check on the NHTSA recalls site as well as NHTSA’s dedicated Takata airbag recall page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season enhancement not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

It has been revealed that the December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

In a recent development, battlefield Studios declared a host of fresh changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

According to recent reports, the focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an glitch that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

In a recent development, the patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios claims should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Industry observers note that some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect upcoming maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage.
  • In a recent development, but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea.
  • Recent findings suggest that that's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

In a recent development, but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile New York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them.".

Recent findings suggest that that's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the new C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

Sources indicate that "Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller remarked. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

Recent findings suggest that the company is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he mentioned. Spyker aims to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is.".

Muller claims approximately 40 percent of his latest buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

In a recent development, “If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller mentioned. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more notable than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker.".

In a recent development, another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The organization competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

It has been revealed that "Absolutely," Muller said. "We'd love to go back in racing." Muller says Spyker is preparing to re-enter endurance racing, although he stopped short of announcing a timeline, championship, or confirmed race entry. He certainly likes the idea of seeing his latest creation on the track. More importantly, he's already started putting people in place to make it happen.

"I actually hired my former GT2 race director again," Muller said. "He started a week ago today.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Social media influencers claim that having a “ferritin face” may indicate you’re low in iron.

Sources indicate that ferritin is a protein that helps your body store iron. You need iron in order to make healthy red blood cells, which carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Iron is also vital for bone marrow, organs, healthy muscles, and brain development.

As “ferritin face” makes its way across social media platforms, users are describing several tell-tale signs, including:.

Industry observers note that people have also shared images of their face before and after taking iron supplements or getting an iron infusion. Videos about “ferritin face” have garnered millions of views on various platforms.

However, medical professionals state that your appearance alone is not enough to diagnose iron deficiency.

“It’s notable to understand that ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis, nor is it a confirmed symptom of iron deficiency. While some people with iron deficiency can appear pale due to low hemoglobin levels in their red blood cells, there are many other symptoms to consider,” stated Daniel Atkinson, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and clinical lead at Treated.

“Notably, these symptoms are also present in many different conditions, and their presence does not necessarily mean iron deficiency anemia or even low ferritin levels. Similar features are seen in people with iron processing and absorption issues, such as gluten intolerance, or in urgent sudden blood loss scenarios,” added Jonathan Jennings, MD, board certified internist at Medical Offices of Manhattan.

Iron deficiency can affect your skin and appearance. These signs are often subtle, but may include:.

In some ways, the social media videos are correct. Your skin and face can change when your iron levels are low.

“The facial signs people point to, like pale skin and a washed-out look, mostly come from anaemia, when your haemoglobin has dropped. But iron deficiency and anaemia aren’t the same thing,” noted Thom Phillips, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and Chief Medical Officer at Forth. “By the time low iron shows on your face, your stores are usually close to empty.”.

It is important to speak with a healthcare professional, who will run blood tests such as a complete blood count and ferritin levels.

It is also key not to take iron supplements without first checking with your healthcare professional, because having too much iron in your body can also cause negative effects.

Too little and too much iron could raise your risk of infection, which is why it’s important not to take supplements without medical supervision.

The signs and symptoms of iron deficiency can depend on whether you are anemic or not. Some of the early signs may include:.

“These symptoms typically occur because your body produces fewer red blood cells, which results in less oxygen being delivered throughout your body, making you feel tired and weak,” remarked Atkinson.

Less common symptoms may include:.

While your facial appearance can be a sign that something isn’t right, healthcare professionals consider other symptoms and how you feel overall.

They also rely on blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

“The misinformation is the idea that you can spot it yourself. That leads to two problems: people with low iron who look fine assume they’re OK, and people who look tired start taking iron supplements they don’t need,” said Phillips.

Atkinson also noted that factors such as different settings and environmental conditions can affect how your face appears.

That being stated, the “ferritin face” trend may help bring awareness to certain symptoms and when to get them checked.

“[This] trend may raise some awareness about iron deficiency anemia and how low iron levels can impact daily life,” mentioned Atkinson.

In a recent development, “Fatigue and lightheadedness are common side effects of low iron, but it manifests in other ways too, such as paler skin or increased hair shedding, which can be concerning for many people. If you experience these symptoms, you should let your doctor know so they can help treat the condition appropriately,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that after feeding as many spy shots as I could into some AI models, we ended up with the images you see here. If they’re accurate, they show a commercial-ready EV that’s meant to attract upcoming fleet buyers looking to ditch diesel in Western markets while serving as a direct, 1:1 replacement for domestic fleet operators already putting Porter pickups to work.

Those operators will probably feel a little safer behind the wheel of the latest truck, too. Hyundai has worked a short hood and crash structure into the bodywork where a conventional “flat” cabover now sits – a move that seems to point both to a commitment to provide better front-end protection to the truck’s occupants and an intent to at least take an honest run at the Euro NCAP crash standards.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, we don’t really know anything about the upcoming Korean pickup – but it’s a safe bet that the next-generation Porter will benefit from some of the technology that’s been baked into the Hyundai Motor Group’s E-GMP.S commercial vehicle platform that underpins the Kia PV vehicles. Those ship with 51.5 and 71.2 kWh battery options sending electrons to 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motors, and while that’s far from a guarantee, it’s not nothing, either.

That’s my take, anyway – what’s yours? Will the Hyundai Porter EV make its way to the West on an AWD version of the E-GMP.S platform, or will it remain a regional model running on one of the firm’s hybrid platforms? Let us know in the comments.

Latest Update: Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • Industry observers note that that absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

Industry observers note that that absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench indicates they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, remarked in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Recent findings suggest that reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

Industry observers note that the robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

Sources indicate that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

The unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Industry observers note that nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took.
  • In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Industry observers note that nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took. They sometimes wonder whether choosing differently might have made them more satisfied with their lives. Regret is, to some extent, part of almost everyone's life. If we marry, we may eventually regret it; if we do not, we may remain alone and regret that too. If we emigrate, we may regret leaving; if we stay and endure our circumstances, we may regret that as well. Whether we remain in a tedious job or choose another, whether we speak our minds to those around us or keep silent, we may still end up regretting our choices.

In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state. We choose things that promise pleasure, yet such choices never lead to lasting joy or satisfaction; what is thrilling today may become mundane and tedious by tomorrow. Boredom inevitably returns, leaving us to lament the choices we made and wish we had chosen differently. To break this cycle of regret and boredom, "A" offers an intriguing proposal: much like farmers who rotate crops to prevent soil erosion, individuals should constantly alter their approach to life—avoiding fixation on any single experience—in order to mitigate boredom. Praising the character of Don Juan—the seductive, womanizing figure from Mozart’s opera—"A" champions the rejection of all commitments as a means to banish boredom and regret. In the same volume, Kierkegaard introduces another character, Johannes, who employs psychological tactics to seduce a young woman named Cordelia, gradually cultivating her affection. He uses strategies such as maintaining distance, employing silence, sowing doubt, and stirring the other person’s emotions—all of which he finds deeply pleasurable.

It has been revealed that in the second part, Kierkegaard writes through another persona, Judge Wilhelm. He recommends that “A” choose an ethical and committed life. A significant portion of this section addresses marriage. Wilhelm argues that only a stable, committed relationship can prevent the initial fire of love and passion from quickly burning out, allowing it instead to endure. Through Wilhelm's voice, Kierkegaard writes that our choices shape our ultimate selves—an idea later further developed within existentialist philosophy. By employing pseudonymous characters, Kierkegaard deliberately avoids taking sides, leaving the conclusion to the reader. Ultimately, he presents choice and regret as fundamental components of human existence [1].

Recent findings suggest that now, we explore the neurological mechanisms underlying the persistent human experience of regret. In their book The Molecule of More, Lieberman and Long discuss two brain circuits—the mesolimbic and the mesocortical—both of which utilize dopamine as a neurotransmitter. The first circuit primarily drives "wanting," motivation, and the anticipation of a reward; it is not about the pleasure itself but rather the anticipated pleasure expected from a given stimulus. The second circuit activates top-down pathways for impulse control, enabling consideration of the future consequences of one's decisions and desires. From an evolutionary perspective, this capacity has allowed humans to transcend immediate, relatively simple responses and plan for the attainment of long-term goals. However, this simplified model of the reward system’s neurology suggests that repetition of a stimulus leads to a diminished reward—driven by a decline in dopamine levels and function within the mesolimbic system—thereby shifting attention and motivation toward fresh rewards [2].

Although the prefrontal cortex is primarily responsible for logical reasoning, evaluation, and behavioral regulation, certain regions within it also play a role in generating feelings of regret. A 2004 study revealed that individuals with damage to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), unlike healthy controls, did not report experiencing regret or anticipating negative outcomes during a gambling task. Additionally, other brain areas, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampus, contribute to the experience of regret by enabling the mental simulation of alternative, unlived scenarios [3].

Industry observers note that in an intriguing paper published in Science Advances in 2023, researchers examined the distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the ventral striatum, and dopaminergic neurons in counterfactual thinking in monkeys. Their findings indicated that the brain can represent not only the reward actually received but also the value of a reward that could have been obtained through a different choice [4]. This suggests that, at times, the source of our regret is not an event that actually occurred in real life, but rather an event that never took place, yet one whose possibility the mind has retained. In effect, we may find ourselves mourning a life we ​​never lived.

In conclusion, the human brain is designed to anticipate the future outcomes of decisions we might have made and to compare those potential results with our current situation. While this capacity can aid in making better future choices, it can also foster a chronic sense of regret. This trait leads us to constantly evaluate our present circumstances against hypothetical alternatives—lamenting the paths we did not take. In the modern era, this inclination has been exacerbated by the rise of social media, which offers numerous opportunities for social comparison and exposes us to constant reminders of "alternative" lives. Observing the lives, homes, cities, and joys of others can trigger anxiety that we are perpetually falling behind.

It has been revealed that here, it helps to distinguish this phenomenon into two types: 1) Constructive Regret, which helps us recognize past mistakes and make better decisions moving forward; and 2) Ruminative Regret, which traps individuals in a cycle of constantly comparing their actual lives with hypothetical scenarios or the lives of others—without necessarily leading to any constructive action or decision. Since it is impossible to experience every life possibility or to know for certain whether a different choice would have been better, we can take the message of the second part of Either/Or to heart: By committing fully to our own lives, rather than constantly dwelling on lost possibilities, we can liberate ourselves from the anxiety and the wearying melancholy of regret.

1. Kierkegaard, S., Hannay, A., & Eremita, V. (2004). Either/Or: A Fragment of Life. Penguin Books Limited.

2. Lieberman, D. Z. and M. E. Long (2018). The Molecule of More: How a Single Chemical in Your Brain Drives Love, Sex, and Creativity--and Will Determine the Fate of the Human Race, BenBella Books.

In a recent development, 3. Camille N, Coricelli G, Sallet J, Pradat-Diehl P, Duhamel JR, Sirigu A. The involvement of the orbitofrontal cortex in the experience of regret. Science. 2004 May 21;304(5674):1167-70.

4. Yun M, Nejime M, Kawai T, Kunimatsu J, Yamada H, Kim HR, Matsumoto M. Distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum, and dopamine neurons in counterfactual thinking of decision outcomes. Sci Adv. 2023 Aug 9;9(32):eadh2831.
