Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout.
  • In a recent development, that information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data.
  • "This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout. The tires use a sensor that looks a lot like a Dexcom G7 to feed temperature, air pressure, acceleration, and identification data to a vehicle's computers.

In a recent development, that information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data. For example, swap your summer tires for squishier winter rubber, and a compatible car could recognize the change and automatically adjust how its electronic controls intervene, leaving you free to imagine a world where maybe we all just drove better.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07011.

"This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani. The sensor, weighing just 13 grams, is bonded to the tire's inner liner beneath the tread using a specially developed adhesive and rubber housing. The process was developed using learnings from Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System, which uses foam inside the tire to absorb sound waves and reduce cabin vibration. The sensor must survive extreme temperatures, constant flexing, and the insane lateral g-forces that tires are susceptible to at over 200 mph. Engineers explained that its battery is designed to outlast the tire and enters a low-power sleep mode during extended storage.

Recent findings suggest that the more inspiring part is what the car does with the information it gathers. As we found in our recent all-weather tire comparison test, summer, winter, and all-season tires perform dramatically differently. Yet a vehicle's electronic controls are generally calibrated around its original equipment, using things like wheel speed sensors that aren’t as close to the road surface as the Cyber Tyre. Instead, it identifies the specific tire installed at each corner, allowing it to use different wheel-slip targets. And with the sensor attached to the inside of the tire, the data informing those systems is closer to the road surface than ever.

We sampled the technology at Las Vegas Motor Speedway in two Mercedes-AMG GT63 S four-doors wearing Cyber Tyre-equipped P Zero MS all-season tires.

The first exercise had us pin the throttle through a corner from 40 mph using three different traction-control calibrations, all on the same P Zero MS all-season tires. The first, intended for ultra-high-performance summer tires, was overly restrictive, cutting power before the tires could deliver much acceleration. The second, calibrated for winter tires, permitted considerably more wheelspin, making the AMG easy to slide. Despite that setting being the most fun (and our favorite), Cyber Tyre delivered a happy medium, allowing more controlled acceleration without either extreme.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07011.

This is where Cyber Tyre begins to make the case against selectable drive modes. The same car, wearing the same tires, just behaved three different ways without any mechanical changes. It's not going to replace the button that stiffens your dampers or changes your exhaust note, but it could eventually make some traction-related settings redundant.

The second AMG demonstrated ABS braking from 65 mph. With Cyber Tyre integration active, our stopping distance improved by 0.9 meter, or about three feet, according to Pirelli's instrumentation. That's not dramatically different, but still a measurable improvement.

Of course, these demonstrations weren't proof that Cyber Tyre can outperform a conventional system already calibrated for the correct tires. And the technology isn't smart enough to know it's snowing just because the tires are cold. But the distinction is that Cyber Tyre can give the car information about its tires without the driver doing anything. That could be super useful as tires wear, temperatures change, or owners swap between summer and winter sets. Pirelli is also developing tire-wear estimates using its sensor data, which could prove useful for fleet operators managing hundreds of vehicles.

Industry observers note that pirelli and Bosch announced their development partnership in 2024, and the technology has already appeared in vehicles from McLaren and Pagani. Pirelli executives say a substantially higher-volume application should be announced in the first half of 2027, with production expected in 2028. So it's possible this tech could arrive in models as common as a Ford pickup.

Pirelli is also investing approximately $1.2 billion to expand its Rome, Georgia, manufacturing facility, where Cyber Tyre-equipped products will be produced alongside conventional tires. By 2033, the firm expects annual production capacity to reach six million tires and plans to add up to 1000 engineering jobs.

Recent findings suggest that they also recently confirmed that China's state-owned Sinochem, formerly Pirelli's largest shareholder, reduced its ownership to 13.6 percent in November. The Italian government has restricted Sinochem's influence and specifically prohibited sharing Cyber Tyre data with entities connected to the Chinese government. Following those governance changes, Pirelli received U.S. authorization to market the technology here. Not that anyone was worried about a Pagani Utopia Roadster being a boon of classified information.

According to recent reports, cyber Tyre isn't about to take the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes out back to shoot them. There are plenty of reasons to let drivers decide how their cars behave. But after experiencing three dramatically different calibrations in the same AMG, it's easy to see why some of those decisions might eventually be better left to the car. Just make sure we’re able to fully disable them.

In a recent development, austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

The 61 Best New Highlights of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • THE IDEA OF "new" television indicates is a little bit of a tricky one these days.
  • In a recent development, but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong.
  • Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something upcoming, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

THE IDEA OF "new" television indicates is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a substantial way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

In a recent development, but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something upcoming, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the highlights we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Sources indicate that netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO).

Industry observers note that in shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock).

Industry observers note that this show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

Sources indicate that at the very least, Wonder Man is among the best demonstrates Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

In a recent development, one of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

In a recent development, this wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The newly introduced season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best highlights of the year.

Industry observers note that the second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new highlights. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

In a recent development, from the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

According to recent reports, this series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in highlights like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those prepares have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

Jury Duty: Company Retreat (Prime Video).

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Tech giant Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix).

Industry observers note that camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand Newly introduced Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%. And now, you can buy one.

Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

Sources indicate that “The (Tadano) V320RC marks a real breakthrough in the pick & carry industry,” reads the official Tadano launch copy. “Rather than an evolution of existing solutions, it introduces a latest philosophy, with technologies and features capable of setting new benchmarks in the lifting market. Tadano and NMG Italia continue their collaboration in the field, turning real-world experience into new technological solutions to meet the most advanced demands of industrial lifting.”.

According to recent reports, the crane itself is a compact, battery-electric pick-and-carry machine with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Measuring just 5 m long, 2.15 m wide and 2.400 m tall (a meter is about a yard, guys – you got this), the V320RC is designed to bring heavy lifting capability into tight industrial spaces where larger cranes struggle to operate.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced Tadano runs on a 120V, 1,120 Ah li-ion battery pack (that works out to ~134 kWh) and packs a gross vehicle weight of more than 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tones). That number includes 9,500 kg (~10 tons) of removable counterweights that make transport and handling easier for a wider range of customers. Under the hood, a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with what the tech giant calls “an electro-hydraulic control valve” to improve precision and responsiveness while reducing energy consumption.

According to NMG Italia, all that baked-in tech V320RC give them 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes working under equivalent workloads, with enough battery capacity to support several days of operation between charges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the Fast & Furious franchise taught us anything, it’s that there’s always another gear, and there’s no such thing as a bad plot­line. (Also: family.) To honor its silver anniversary, here’s a recap of the F&F universe, as it expanded from the L.A. street-racing scene to encompass every action-film trope, device, and format ever scrawled on a Hollywood studio whiteboard.

The Fast and the Furious (2001).

Cop Brian O’Connor infiltrates the L.A. import-car scene to bust hijackers who steal DVD players and at least one sweet 13-inch TV/VCR combo. He bonds with bald kingpin Dominic Toretto, then lets him go. Executives smell a sequel. Toretto has other prepares: The Chronicles of Riddick. Danger to manifold: 10/10.

Now a fugitive with a Nissan Skyline but no visible means of support, Brian joins the feds to catch a drug lord who tortures a corrupt cop with the ol’ rat-in-the-ice-bucket trick. Roman Pearce replaces Dom as the bald guy at the emotional core. Camaro jumps onto yacht. Danger to manifold: 5/10.

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

Brian who? Now it’s Sean, a high schooler who looks like he’s 35. Busted for street racing, he’s sent to Tokyo, the capital of street racing. He crosses the yakuza-­connected Drift King and falls in with Han Seoul-­Oh, who can’t stop snacking. Dom cameo as sequel bait. Danger to manifold: 七/10.

Recent findings suggest that dom’s back, and the crew now executes road-train robberies in the Dominican Republic. Brian, now FBI, infiltrates a heroin pipeline. Letty dies. Dom seeks vengeance. A Road Warrior–style chase ends in a killer wheelie, literally. Dom is busted, but a sequel is nigh. Danger to manifold: 3/10.

Industry observers note that street racing? Nah. We’re a heist franchise, dog. Dom’s crew, now fully Hollywood four-quadrant tested, steals a crime lord’s fortune in Brazil. A former wrestler highlights up as DSS agent Luke Hobbs. Bald jokes and legal ambiguity ensue. Everybody walks with $100 million. Danger to manifold: 1.5/10.

Hobbs is back, and we meet British scoundrel number one, Owen Shaw, an ex-SAS mercenary who drives a ramp car that flips police cruisers like a spatula. Letty is alive (huh?), with amnesia, and on Shaw’s payroll. Gisele dies. (Who’s Gisele again?) Danger to manifold: –10/10.

Jason Statham (really?) is Deckard Shaw, Owen’s scoundrel brother, who fireballs Dom’s family home. The crew parachutes into Azerbaijan in their cars. A Lykan HyperSport jumps between three Abu Dhabi office towers. Han’s dead (like we believe that). The saddest ending imaginable. Danger to manifold: N/A.

Fate, F9, Fast X, Hobbs & Shaw (2017–23).

According to recent reports, roll call: John Cena. Dame Helen Mirren. Charlize Theron. Jason Momoa. Sir Idris Elba. Old villains are in the crew now. We’re in Cuba (thanks, Obama), Antarctica, a sub­marine, and a Pontiac Fiero in space. Han? Gisele? Both alive. It’s just a parody of action movies now, right? Danger to manifold: $7 billion/10.

According to recent reports, hoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the massive highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

It has been revealed that alongside showing everything coming with this next upgrade, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

Industry observers note that this final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The newly introduced playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

According to recent reports, while The Dahlia is the only latest character appearing in this final Amphoreus patch, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

It has been revealed that something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the latest patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

#132682. Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • In a recent development, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals latest insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but upcoming research challenges this conclusion.

In a recent development, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals latest insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich mentioned in a statement.

The pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

Industry observers note that “There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” stated Schultrich.

Recent findings suggest that double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s currently clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

According to recent reports, the same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

In a recent development, “It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

#132681. Mammograms May Offer Early Insight Into Cardiovascular Disease

Mammograms May Offer Early Insight Into Cardiovascular Disease

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.
  • The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.
  • On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.

The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.

On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.

While BAC is harmless to the breasts, it is associated with a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease. A 2022 study found women with BAC were 51% more likely to develop heart disease or experience a stroke than those without it.

In a recent development, laxmi Mehta, MD, a cardiologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, stated BAC is associated with cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Additionally, BAC has been connected to:.

“The reasons for BAC resulting in higher risks for cardiovascular disease are not definitely determined; however, there are some potential mechanisms, one being that they share similar risk factors that result in vascular injury or metabolic stress that result in vascular calcification and atherosclerosis,” Mehta told Healthline.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center, added that because BAC and heart disease share many of the same risk factors, “calcium in breast arteries therefore suggests disease in the heart (coronary) and brain arteries as well,” he told Healthline.

While 1 in 39 females in the United States dies from breast cancer each year, cardiovascular disease causes one out of every three deaths, resulting in 1 death per minute.

“Cardiovascular disease is still the most common cause of death in premenopausal women,” Richard Reitherman, MD, PhD, a radiologist and medical director of breast imaging at MemorialCare Breast Center at Orange Coast Medical Center, told Healthline.

“The presentation of cardiovascular disease in premenopausal women is notoriously different than in postmenopausal women, primarily [because] there are no typical symptoms such as chest pain.”.

Reitherman stated that a prevalent and common health screening procedure such as a mammogram can lead to the early identification of women with silent cardiovascular disease.

“Cardiovascular outcome studies that have included breast arterial calcifications as a risk factor are increasingly reported in the medical literature,” he stated.

“The hope is that identifying younger women with silent cardiovascular risks [like BAC along with] appropriate integrated risk identification, analysis, and interventions can significantly reduce mortality in this age group.”.

Mehta stated there are several reasons BAC has been overlooked as a risk factor for heart disease.

“Mammograms are completed for assessment of breast cancer, and BAC has been historically an ‘incidental’ finding, which is not clinically relevant from an oncologic standpoint,” she noted.

Additionally, there is no standardization on quantification of BAC severity, nor is it a required component of mammogram reports, noted Mehta.

However, routine reporting of BAC on mammograms is an urgent goal of the American College of Radiology, Society of Breast Imaging, and Medicare, remarked Reitherman.

In fact, it is gaining traction in the United States. A new Maryland law, passed on October 1, requires mammography centers to notify women when a BAC is detected on their mammogram.

“Automated identification and reporting of these calcifications detected on screening mammograms will become increasingly prevalent in the coming months [and] years,” stated Reitherman.

The next step is to identify this group of women to primary care physicians so that appropriate risk evaluation can take place, Reitherman added.

In addition to doctors routinely screening for conditions related to heart disease, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, he hopes BAC will also be routinely considered.

“Under current development are protocols to identify patients needing a cardiologist’s training and expertise to appropriately stratify this group of patients,” mentioned Reitherman.

“The common healthcare behavior [of] having regular mammograms not only reduces risk of morbidity and mortality from breast cancer but will hopefully contribute to the reduction of morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease in younger women.”.

He said this type of integrated healthcare approach demonstrates cross-specialty integration and coordination among women, radiologists, and their healthcare providers to improve women’s lives.

“This is an amazing game-changing opportunity,” Reitherman noted.

Mehta remarked it’s reasonable for women to ask if BAC is present on their mammogram report.

“But if it is not uniformly reported by the radiologist, the individual clinician may not have the answer,” she said.

More research is needed before BAC on mammograms can be used routinely to predict heart disease.

Finding out your BAC could provide additional information to help you and your doctors decide how aggressively to address your cardiovascular risk factors, Chen said.

According to recent reports, reitherman agreed. “The goal of reducing morbidity and mortality from any cause such as cardiovascular disease is based on recognition of risk factors, followed by appropriate lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions,” he mentioned.

#132680. Breaking: I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1013 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In a recent development, I never got a specific memo about how to let go of my children.
  • There is a well-worn path of letting go, which surprisingly begins when a child is a few hours old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In a recent development, I never got a specific memo about how to let go of my children. My parents, as Australians, were more open to this idea than the European parents of many of my contemporaries, most of whom had recently endured the trauma of the holocaust. But even with a different cultural background, I've felt that mothering and letting go is, on so many levels, a contradiction in terms. Mothers receive an intuitive message: You are meant to stay close to your children, to protect them, and to look after them. We assume this means always.

There is a well-worn path of letting go, which surprisingly begins when a child is a few hours old. Lisa Baraitser1 opened my mind to this in her description of the newborn falling asleep. It describes the mother’s response, her feelings and tears as she realizes that her infant’s “first sleeps” hold a deeper meaning as he/she goes “away on their own for the first time.” It’s almost like a jolt, an awareness for the mother that her infant, a mere few hours old, drifts in sleep to a place that she isn’t part of. In the full swing of post-birth, we aren’t really tuned into receiving this message.

Recent findings suggest that this realization would have helped me. It would have informed my understanding of mothering: that one’s child, even at a few hours old, is a separate being. It's a startling and humbling recognition that, as mothers, we don't own our children; we are “there to be left,” as Erna Furman2 puts it.

According to recent reports, we get these messages continually from our children. The child crawls away from us to experience the world, then walks, then goes to preschool. But for the first 11 or so years, we are the ultimate hands-on caregivers. We feed, rock, and change our infants. When they are toddlers and young children, we kiss their skinned knees, and we are at their service all day and during the night to calm their nightmares and their sore tummies. To them, mom is the person who knows how to fix things—everything. We are their person.

This changes when our adolescent teenager surfaces. We become sparring partners, and if we are lucky, we get more than a contemptuous look or that stare. We return to nights of interrupted sleep, as we stay awake all hours waiting for them to come home. We spend a lot of time reflecting on and talking about what’s gotten hold of our child. Why is there no conversation? Why are they so abrupt and rude? Why is it all about their friends? It’s so difficult to reframe this as a process of healthy separation, a letting go, as they wear us out in a new way— with emotional exhaustion. Those of us who want to hold onto the earlier status quo are in trouble.

Industry observers note that the teenage years give us pause for thought. How do we receive the message to back off, that we need to let go? One of the wisest comments that I ever heard about this stage is that a child is like this because he/she can be, because he/she has a mom who can bear it. The child intuits this through continual testing. It’s all part of the separation. It requires us to hold onto the sides of the roller coaster driven by our child, to stay on board and go with it while insisting on some guardrails, believing that our child will return to us one day, albeit in a different form.

Then, as our children approach late teens and early 20s, there are newly introduced challenges and shifts as they hopefully enter the workforce, continue their education, train for a trade or technical career, or go out on his/her own. We become more like roommates on different programs as we navigate home life with another adult. Or they leave home.

Recent findings suggest that the next stage may include our child partnering, and the cycle begins again with their own children. Our next lesson is that it's their turn to make their own family. Are we able to watch and learn with curiosity and gratitude?

It has been revealed that as we look back at our mothering, it’s clear that one of the most key parts of mothering is to intuit when to let go and how: to know that each child is different, and to ask ourselves whether we've been adaptive, accepting, and understanding enough. Have we tried to hold on too long or let them go too soon? Have we used guilt, been a victim, or judged them openly and harshly? Have we encouraged our child at each stage to learn their own place in the world?

In a recent development, how do we get there? Letting go of one’s children is an art form. It takes sensitivity, a lack of ego, and not putting ourselves first.

Sources indicate that my work on ambivalence has guided my understanding of this. Mothering is full of contradictory feelings that can be difficult to bear, that often seize us at any one time, and also renew our love and give us the strength to separate.

It has been revealed that saying goodbye to our 4-year-old at preschool is a bittersweet love. We feel both fury that our 15-year-old arrives home at 4 am without calling and absolute love when he/she walks through the door in one piece. We feel pride and joy when we see our child commit to a partner, but also loss; they belong to someone else now. All of these feelings mean separation.

1. Baraitser, Lisa (2009). Maternal Encounters: The Ethics of Interruption. London, UK: Taylor & Francis.

Industry observers note that 2. Furman, Erna (2001). On Being and Having a Mother. Madison, CT: International Universities Press.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

Short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

George and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

In a recent development, this remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

It has been revealed that bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

Illinois’ Clean Ports Program isn’t just replacing diesel-powered equipment with electric alternatives – instead, the plan also includes Level 2 and DC fast charging, shore power and charging for electrified ships, and comprehensive grid upgrades designed to modernize existing port operations and support the deployment of new electric equipment.

In a recent development, the program takes a holistic approach to port electrification at Chicago’s Illinois International Port District (IIPD), treating energy generation, storage, and deployment as parts of a single connected system. On-site solar helps meet the port’s growing electricity needs while excess power is stored for peak hours, when grid electricity is most expensive. This setup reduces strain on the local grid, and acts as a hedge against rising energy costs.

According to recent reports, for smaller public port districts, replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be an enormous financial undertaking. The Illinois Clean Ports Program helps make those investments possible, bringing cleaner, healthier, zero-emission technology within reach of terminal operators while preparing the state’s ports for a more competitive freight future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new revision. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the fresh patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew newly introduced content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

Recent findings suggest that the Ice Climbing Axe is the only latest weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Sources indicate that easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a significant pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

In a recent development, some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Sources indicate that speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the glitch should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

Industry observers note that physical buttons have a lot going for them. They’re easy to find by feel, satisfying to use, and generally pretty good at staying wherever the automaker installed them. For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited. First, Audi notes in its patent documents with the German government that the switches can deploy at startup, via voice controls, or via gestures. Moving the controls from the screen to the physical switches also provides more total screen room for users. (In one example, the physical bar deploys when a movie opens, leaving more room for the video.).

Ultimately, this could be a great way to meet the demands of more people. Designers love a clean dashboard without physical buttons and switches. Plenty of drivers really love having that switchgear. This system allows owners to pick whatever they want on the fly.

According to recent reports, the timing makes plenty of sense too. Audi has openly noted that it views moving toward more mechanical controls as the right direction. Of course, adding extra complexity to the once-simple idea of buttons also can increase the cost down the line when it comes time for repairs, but even so, this idea is certainly a fascinating solution to a very modern problem.

#132674. Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1959, a sociologist named George Brown led a study of 156 men diagnosed with schizophrenia who had recently been discharged.
  • Recent findings suggest that more studies followed.
  • A 1989 study highlighted that the single best predictor of relapse among patients who’d been hospitalized for depression was their response to the question, “How critical is your spouse of you?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

In 1959, a sociologist named George Brown led a study of 156 men diagnosed with schizophrenia who had recently been discharged. Most went to live with family members: parents, spouses, siblings. A smaller group lived alone in rented rooms. Brown followed them for a year. He found that among those who lived with family, about one-third ended up in the hospital. Of those who lived alone, none did.

Recent findings suggest that more studies followed. Data from a 1976 study suggested that cutting back on time with a critical relative was roughly as protective as antipsychotic medication against relapse in schizophrenia.

A 1989 study highlighted that the single best predictor of relapse among patients who’d been hospitalized for depression was their response to the question, “How critical is your spouse of you?”.

A 1998 meta-analysis found that a critical or overinvolved family was linked to poor outcomes for conditions as diverse as depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders.

What’s interesting is that these aren’t families you’d ordinarily deem “abusive.” The standard framework for assessing family dysfunction today, the adverse childhood experiences framework, doesn’t capture them. These studies examine lesser forms of dysfunction, what many of us would call “normal.”.

I’m going to wager that you’ve never heard of this body of research. As a historian, I find that this raises an equally fascinating question: Why not?

According to recent reports, in the 1960s, psychiatrists were quick to blame parents for mental illness, especially mothers. Schizophrenia was explained by a “schizophrenogenic mother,” autism by a “refrigerator mother.” But the more careful psychiatrists emphasized that the problem was never solely the mother, or solely the father, but the family dynamic that engulfed mother, father, and child.

Recent findings suggest that by the late 1970s, however, parents of patients were tired of being told that their kids’ mental illness was their fault. This era led to the emergence of groups like the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill, founded in 1979 by two Wisconsin mothers whose sons had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Such groups promoted the emerging biological perspective that viewed mental illnesses as brain disorders. Historian Anne Harrington, in Mind Fixers (2019), documents the role such advocacy groups played in popularizing the biomedical view.

Recent findings suggest that by the 1990s, the biomedical model was firmly established in the American psyche. Everything was now a chemical imbalance. Family dynamics seemed to be off the table for good.

Today, psychiatrists claim that they’ve moved away from narrow biological reductionism to accept a “biopsychosocial” model, one that explores the whole range of factors that create and sustain mental illness. You’d think the family would have been put back on the map. It wasn’t, with one partial exception.

In a recent development, advocates of the biopsychosocial framework often use the adverse childhood experiences framework to assess family precursors to mental illness. But its entries center on extreme forms of trauma, abuse, and neglect. The lesser forms of family dysfunction that psychiatrists once sought to understand remain largely off the table.

It has been revealed that to my knowledge, only one research tradition has kept the family in view from the 1950s to today: “expressed emotion” research. It has built a robust body of findings.

In a recent development, its core finding, put at the most general level, is that high “expressed emotion” in families is a strong predictor of relapse in numerous illnesses, including schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders. To break it down a bit more:.

1. Criticism: When the family member expresses constant disapproval, or when they insinuate that the person is lazy or selfish.

2. Hostility: When the family member disparages the person for who they are, or when they believe that the person could “snap out of it.”.

3. Emotional overinvolvement: When the family reveals excessive concern for the person’s well-being, and when they convey the message that the person is “unable to cope” with the world.

A 1994 analysis of 25 studies, covering more than 1,300 patients around the world, found that the link between expressed emotion and relapse was “overwhelming.” More recent work, by researchers such as Preethi Premkumar, has extended these findings to people who have never been diagnosed with anything, showing that young adults with mild psychosis-like traits (“schizotypy”) see their relatives as more critical, and the feeling of being criticized goes along with depression and anger.

According to recent reports, as I know from my own experience, having a loved one with schizophrenia or other serious mental disorder can be overwhelming, taxing, and uncertain. It can create a mix of intense feelings like pity, guilt, and anger.

According to recent reports, proponents of expressed emotion research emphasize that the solution isn’t to lay more shame and blame on families, but counseling and education. Clinical practice guidelines universally recommend family counseling.

Can families cause mental illness? The jury’s still out. But they can sustain mental health crises and make them more likely to recur. That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t go home for the holidays. But it may help to be aware of how family dynamics can affect your mental health.

Breaking: Wasps recognize faces—and it keeps them from killing each other

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that wasps can recognize faces.
  • Industry observers note that “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, stated in a statement.
  • The team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that wasps can recognize faces. But don’t worry. They may not be telling human faces apart the way that cows can. The stingy insects tell their nestmates apart by recognizing different color patterns on their faces, so they know the difference between mama wasp and papa wasp or a friend versus a foe. A study published today in the journal Cell details how they use specialized brain cells to pull this off.

Industry observers note that “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, stated in a statement. “These groups of neurons are all firing, and each neuron has a slightly different preference for one face or another.”.

The team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates). These roughly half-inch long bugs are found from southern parts of Canada through Florida and Texas. Their name comes from the paper-like nests made of hexagonal cells that they often construct under building eaves and on the ceilings of porches. Paper wasps also have silk that shine under UV light, giving these nests a secretive fluorescent glow.

In a recent development, female northern paper wasps use facial recognition to remember another wasp’s place in the nest’s hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, recognizing faces helps maintain social order, without a constant battle for dominance.

It has been revealed that wasps may be using a method for facial recognition that’s similar to how primates (including humans) tell faces apart, even though both methods evolved independently. Even with brains about the size of a single rice grain, Jernigan said that wasps are “able to do this incredibly complex task of remembering and recalling individuals.” They do this by spotting the differences between the color patterns on one wasp face versus another, with the help of specialized neurons.

Wasps can also perform something called social eavesdropping. When two wasps fight to establish dominance in the nest hierarchy, one wasps can watch the two unknown wasps quarrel. Once that spectator wasp sees one of them, it will know whether or not it needs to fight for dominance.

“They will treat the winner of that fight independently in a third interaction differently than they would the loser,” Jernigan explained. “Despite having these small brains and relatively simple vision, they have these really complex social lives that revolve around this specialized ability to recognize each other.”.

According to the team, understanding this facial recognition could help us understand human brain systems as well.

In a recent development, “This system, hopefully, holds the potential to help us understand our own brains as we study the circuit connections and the role of experience in giving rise to identity recognition,” Jernigan mentioned. “It’s really remarkable that they have this kind of really human-like or primate-like ability that you wouldn’t typically expect for an insect. And I think it’s almost unbelievable that they have some of the similar kind of neural computations for doing a similar task as we do. It takes a tremendous amount of neural connections to do something similar in a primate.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AS LONG AS there are movies, there will be action movies. Why? Because no young girl or boy grows up pretending to be a damsel in distress or a sidekick. They all want to punch, draw swords, and run toward the danger. They are the heroes and the future directors, choreographers, and performers who bring these imaginations to life.

In a recent development, and to the incredulity of your father (who insists no movie will ever top First Blood) the action genre hasn’t slipped on it’s roundhouse kick. If anything, we are now experiencing another golden age of ass-kicking cinema. While there are obvious developments in VFX technology, which have allowed for larger set pieces and more realistic thrills, much of what makes a great acton film a great action film hasn’t changed: painstaking choreography, fearless stunt performers/actors, and clear cinematography (and not that Taken fence jumping bullshit.).

The only thing that’s changed are the names and faces. Legend action directors like Ang Lee, John Woo, Robert Clouse, and Zhang Yimou (still going strong) have given way to newer arrivals like Gareth Evans, Chad Stahelski, and Christopher Nolan. And performers like Bruce Lee, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and Arnold have changed to Tony Jaa, Iko Uwais, and Charlize Theron.

In a recent development, if anything, the fights are becoming more brutal, more carefully choreographed, and more ambitious. And international actors and directors are finally getting increased attention (and direction) in a Hollywood overly-saturated with slapstick cinematography and post-production punches.

Here’s hoping for more John Wicks, more Raids, and more Atomic Blondes in the future. Until then, here is, in no particular order, the 36 best action movies ever made.

John Rambo would become increasingly cartoonish as the sequels went on, but in the original, he was just a scared veteran trying to survive out in the real world.

According to recent reports, the Raid was more frenzied, but the sequel (also written and directed by Gareth Evans) got grand, introducing an intricate crime-drama plot. Didn’t matter: Redemption is brilliantly violent, a ballet of broken bones, perfect punches and crazy car chases.

Sources indicate that the film marked the breakout moment for Muy Thai martial artist Tony Jaa and the beginning of one of the best action franchises ever. There’s not a lot of fakery in Jaa’s fight scenes. Dudes are getting punched for real.

The second film is more dialogue-heavy, but the first half is essentially nonstop action … and it’s a good thing the Crazy 88 fight is in black and white, because it’d almost be too bloody to watch otherwise.

It has been revealed that what should have been Jason Bourne’s final adventure is a thrilling, satisfying conclusion to this kinetic trilogy. Director Paul Greengrass and star Matt Damon permanently reshaped how we think of the globetrotting espionage thriller. James Bond is still playing catch-up.

Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation (2015).

You can’t go wrong with any in this series – though it has only gotten better as the years have gone along – but the introduction of Rebecca Ferguson to this series just amped up the emotional stakes.

Keanu Reeves’ first of two masterful franchises on this list, John Wick gave us a mournful 21st-century assassin who won’t let his grief get in the way of shooting every bad guy in the head at point-blank range.

Bruce Lee was popular before this film, but this is what sent him into the stratosphere. Well-made from start to finish, and absolutely unrelenting. The best part about it is that there isn’t a gun to be found in the whole film.

It has been revealed that ong-Bak gave us Tony Jaa and Muy Thai, and Ip Man gave us Donnie Yen and Wing Chun. While Yen had been in many other great action films previously (check out Kill Zone — S.P.L.), its the Ip Man films that will define his legacy, the character forever his—the semi-biographical person of Ip Man, Bruce Lee’s trainer. Though the films can feel a bit jingoistic at times (they’re basically Hong Kong’s Rambo), the fight scenes are femur-breaking legendary.

Recent findings suggest that zhang Yimou’s magnum opus, Daggers is maybe more love story than a martial arts film—and so the most action-packed love story of all time—but “love story” is no cinematic pejorative. The film features the most colorful and vibrant cinematography of any film on this list. Action is a visual genre. And no film here is more pleasing to the eyes.

John Woo’s Hollywood career wasn’t as sparkling or consistent as fans would have hoped, but this late-‘80s peak remains a glorious salute to melodramatic plotting and poetic shootouts. Chow Yun-fat made for a fierce, soulful assassin — and, never forget, The Killer is where Woo began his obsession with dove-filled action scenes, which have been parodied everywhere from 21 Jump Street to Scary Movie 2.

It has been revealed that oh, don’t dare not think of this as an action movie. The existential dread of Ridley Scott’s original is replaced by James Cameron’s trademark intensity, and even though this has aliens and spaceship, this is as concentrated a dose of thriller mania as you will find. You’re gripping your chair just thinking about it, aren’t you?

George Miller had been mulling a fresh Mad Max film for years, and clearly, he spent that time coming up with every possible permutation of a chase sequence. This movie remains thrilling, almost insane, four years later.

Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

Recent findings suggest that because of Ang Lee’s prestige and the glamorous international cast, there is sometimes a sense that this film is bland, good-for-you Important Filmmaking. But watch it again today. This movie is iconic for a reason: it's a blast, and a euphoric ride.

Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991).

If the first installment was more of a gritty thriller, then T2 is where director James Cameron cranked up the action spectacle. (That’s the kind of thing that happens when you have a much bigger budget.) Harnessing the power of then-new CG technology, this sequel threw down a challenge at the start of the ‘90s that other blockbuster filmmakers struggled to answer.

Men in Black is that perfect mix of boot-chasing, gun-firing acton with so much outer-wordly originality, Hollywood is still trying to suck every last ounce of life-force out of the 1997 original. Can we just leave the classics alone?

Recent findings suggest that yes, the car chases are as amazing as you’ve heard, but what’s striking today is how well this holds up as a cop procedural. Steve McQueen was an incredible movie star, and he was never better than he was here.

Sources indicate that popeye Doyle is the perfect action star for the ‘70s: grizzled, cranky, morally compromised, not the least bit likable, but absolutely tenacious about getting the bad guy, even if it’s for reasons he can’t even necessarily comprehend. Gene Hackman was at the absolute peak of his powers at this point.

Hollywood remade Akira Kurosawa’s masterpiece as The Magnificent Seven. It couldn’t compare: Not only is Seven Samurai an epic of scope and scale, it’s one of the most emotionally nuanced of action movies, featuring a slew of characters you come to care deeply about.

Recent findings suggest that michael Mann’s epic is the culmination of everything he’d been working toward his entire career; the years since still feel like his own response to it. Everybody remembers the diner scene, but the bank heist sequence feels like a magic trick even more today.

Industry News: Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.
  • It has been revealed that the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine.
  • In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

It has been revealed that the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

Sources indicate that “People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” said Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who strategy to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:.

According to recent reports, when the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is important to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is important for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” mentioned Finn.

She added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an important source of iodine for the same reasons.

However, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

Sources indicate that plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

According to recent reports, however, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

Industry observers note that check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

Recent findings suggest that “Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” stated Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”.

Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong
